## Macaw

Macaw was a species of a loud and brightly-colored parrot found in the jungles and hot humid forests in South Faerûn and on the continent of Maztica.

Description
Macaws were renowned for their loud colors and the ability to memorize and imitate humanoid speech. Like other parrots, they had strong claws and beaks used for climbing and their toes allowed the birds to handle small objects.

Ecology
The macaw diet consisted of fruits, nuts, and a small quantity of meat.

In Maztica, locals often trained a number of exotic beasts. Parrots and macaws were among the most common. Their brightly colored feathers were used in the region's unique pluma magic. The more colorful the feather was, the more valuable it was to a pluma-user. Macaw plumage was gathered from birds caught by masterfully-crafted snares after the hunters quickly wrung their necks. These feathers were used by crafters to weave bright and brilliant macaw cloaks for Maztican nobles.

Pluma spells of bird charm II could be used to tame and command Maztican birds, including macaws.

Habitats
In the Shining South, macaws and other parrots swarmed the Forest of Amtar in Dambrath.

Domesticated macaws could be found in the ancient city of Cursrah in the Calim Caliphates.

Beyond Prime Material plane, macaws inhabited the jungle Domais of Dread – Sri Raji.

History
In the, a Maztican deity Qotal used talking macaws to guide his chosen cleric Erixitl during the period of war between the conquistadors of Amn and the men of the True World, corrupted by Lolth's shadowy manipulations and the cruel god of war Zaltec.

## Malatran sign language

Malatran sign language was a large family of distinct non-verbal languages used by the various races of the Malatran Plateau. Each tribe on the Plateau had their own sign language, which were distinct enough from one another that mixing them could not be done.

History
The various sign languages used by tribes on the Malatran Plateau developed over time from the necessity of hunters needing a way to communicate to one another without alerting their prey. In an effort to better facilitate communication, one form of sign language on the Plateau was developed by the lacerials and taught to a select few tribes.

## Malune Nalonkrivar

Malune Nalonkrivar was the Magister from  to .

Appearance
He was tall and handsome, with a beard, icy blue eyes, and sharp features.

Personality
Malune was described as a master of intrigues, and a smooth-tongued man.

Possessions
As the Magister, Malune employed little beyond his own spellbook and a ring of flying. The remainder of his wealth was cached throughout Faerûn, with his possessions previous to becoming the Magister in particular being in a ruined castle.

History
Before his tenure, Malune had been an ambassador to Thay, Tharsult, Mulhorand, and Tethyr; however, he was not seen as adequate, because of his reluctance to bluster and threaten. On the day he was offered the position of the Magister, Malune was the target of an assassination attempt; Azuth carried the two of them away from the assassins, up over the night sky of Calimport, through a ceiling that turned to gas temporarily. Malune, viewing his previous life as forfeit, accepted.

As the Magister, Malune traveled extensively, stopping only to aid mages and experience local delights; his acumen with business ensured he never had any trouble with money, while his power was sufficient to casually win duels. He died in the Tunland, after the winter snows of  swelled the swamps; on stopping to rest, he accidentally wandered into a black dragon's ambush. The dragon, Constulgrael, decapitated him with a single bite before he could do anything.

Rumors & Legends
It is said many of the mages Malune stopped to aid were young, comely women; Malune judged this was so, and viewed it as a sign of Mystra's favor, for she brought such delights close by.

## Maldiglas Turntower

Maldiglas Turntower was the Magister from  to . He created a number of refuges.

Appearance
He was six and a half feet tall, with sharp brown eyes and a firm stride.

Personality
Maldiglas was polite, and used to be humble and straight about the limits of his powers. Over time, he developed a bit of a superior attitude as he became a more accomplished mage.

Possessions
He was never seen without a staff half again as tall as himself.

Abilities
Maldiglas soon found he was susceptible to just about all diseases he encountered.

History
Originally from Sembia, his family moved to Amn and then to Chessenta over trouble with an inheritance. As a youth, he decided to become a mage when a mage named Kheldivur died in front of him, spellbook in hand; Maldiglas took the book and resolved to become a wizard. From the start, he decided he wanted to be independant from rulers, and to travel broadly, hoping to see as much of Faerûn as possible. During his travels, he was attacked by Qilder Yarven, whom he defeated, gaining in the process the mantle of the Magister.

After a prayer to Mystra which she answered, he embroiled himself in politics, calling on rulers uninvited, often cowing them into removing oppressive laws that were an obstacle to sorcerous learning, or cajoling them into peace agreements on terms that best suited his ends. He also publicly reproached mages who employed their magic in petty bullyings, and strongly encouraged the plunder of old tombs and older magic throughout Faerûn. His most important project, however, was the creation of a number of refuges, which eventually drained all of his lifeforce.

Rumors
Maldiglas was said to have been greatly rewarded by Mystra for giving up all of his lifeforce to the task of creating the Refuges. However, his ultimate fate after Mystra's Choice remained unknown as of the late 14 century DR.

## Maxiladanarr Torstren

Maxiladanarr Torstren was the Magister from  to .

Appearance
Of average height, Maxiladanarr's hair was always unruly. He had a weathered face and sharp eyes.

Personality
He viewed wizards' duels as wasteful.

History
Maxiladanarr had explored much of Faerûn by both expedition and through magical scrying. He became the Magister after slaying two Red Wizards who summoned monsters to savage Ulraen of Eltabbar, after he slew Veldribold of Calimport, who had slain the previous Magister. His first act was to blast apart his own tower; he always hid both his magic and himself afterwards, making many believe he was actually dead. He traveled often by gates, and did not take a home again, working against the clock in expectation that some young upstart would catch up to him and take the mantle away. His main project was the breeding of a number of clans, akin to the project of another previous archmage, Olohmber Starnardyn.

Maxiladanarr covertly manipulated them into arranged marriages, and let a profusion of magical scrolls find their way to these new clan members. He ultimately perished in an avalanche.

## Maztapan Island

Maztapan Island was a large island that rose up from the water immediately east of the Gulf of Kultaka and later claimed as territory of the Borderlands and its capital, New Waterdeep.

Geography
Maztapan Island was a dry island located at the southwestern end of the Gulf of Cordell in Maztica. The island was just off the coast of the Maztican nation of Kultaka. With the fall of Nexal and colonization, Maztapan was claimed by New Waterdeep, and it neighbored the territories of New Amn.

History

In the, in the days that preceded the Night of Wailing, an Amnian vessel called Helm's Choice, under the command of Captain Quintara, traveled past the strait between Maztapan and the mainland. The ship was ambushed by a curious giant squid, who thought the boat to be a new and exciting edible prey that had wandered into its territory. The sea beast was scared off, but Helm's Choice sustained damage and was forced to land.

In the, twelve trade ships from Waterdeep were denied docking at the New Amnian colony of Helmsport because of the Council of Six's newly imposed restrictions on transoceanic trade. The ships sailed further west until they had their first landfall on the island of Maztapan. Soon after, the Waterdhavian ships crossed the Gulf of Kultaka and established the colony of the New Waterdeep, naming the claimed territory as the Borderlands. Eventually, Maztapan Island became a mooring site for New Waterdeep.

In the, the first settlement of the New Waterdeep was attacked and razed to the ground by Kultakan raiders. Survivors of the attack fled to Trythosford and eventually rebuilt New Waterdeep on Maztapan Island by Eleint 4 of the .

## Maritime Tales of Faerûn

Maritime Tales of Faerûn was a book that collected stories, legends, and folktales of the seafaring folk of Faerûn, published sometime before 1372 DR.

Contents
One of the notable tales in the book talked about ghost ships. The book talked about the violent naval history of the Sword Coast, bloody battles between navies, pirates, monsters, and merchant ships. Thousands of vessels found their final rest at the bottom of the Sea of Swords over the course of centuries. But not all of the perished ships remained dead. Tavern tales talked about Those Who Sail Forever, but not before making warding hand signs against evil and ill luck. They believed that even mentioning the name of Those Who Sail Forever brought the undead's attention to the sailor.

Some doubted existence of ghost ships as some slavers and pirates were known to wear skull masks and travel under the shroud of night or fog. Some believed that failed ensorcelled ship hulls and magical energies from special enchanted cargo all interacted and became corrupted, creating the ghost ships, keeping them afloat and helmed by skeletons or zombies. Their magical nature became apparent when these ghost ships sailed without sails. Another type of ghost ship was a type of ghostly wraith-like apparition, an incorporeal copy of its former self.

Another source of these sea apparitions was the Bitch Queen herself, goddess Umberlee, who tasked the ghosts with returning long-drowned magic items into the hands of surface dwellers. These lucky sailors, in turn, filled seaside taverns with stories of such findings, attracting greedy men into Umberlee's clutches.

Finally, the most famous ghost ship recorded in the book was the Red Prow of Calimport. Once, a slaver ship that sank under the weight of its gold and gems. According to eyewitnesses, the Red Prow carried wraiths and "wielder things" that rode men like horses. Another greatly feared ghost ships was Dread Pirate Gonchklas' caravel, the Ravager. The ship was manned by skeletons and sea zombies, attacking every ship it encountered in the sea.

## Manor Atheon

History
The manor was once inhabited by Lord Sarnil Atheon. The nobleman famously went mad after a mysterious sea fog shrouded the villa for five days straight. Driven insane, Sarnil used the Atheon ancestral greatsword to slaughter his entire family. Since then, Manor Atheon was left unoccupied. On occasion, the strange fog returned and hung over the villa. Mad Sarnil Atheon's howls were heard echoing from the fog as ghosts of his wife and children could be seen eternally fleeing from their murderer. Each fog caused the scene of grisly murder to repeat itself as the ghosts fled across the villa's halls, dripping blood along the way.

## Malsheem

Malsheem, also known as the Citadel of Hell, was an infernal fortress-city found in Nessus the deepest layer of the Nine Hells. It was the home of Asmodeus― the Faerûnian god of indulgence and lord of the Nine Hells―along with his army of infernal guardians.

Asmodeus' city was not accessible by teleportation and could not be viewed by scrying, unless the archdevil allowed as such. The only known portal that led into Malsheem was found deep within Cania, which was guarded by 9,999 gelugons at all times.

Description
The citadel of Malsheem was beyond impressive in design and scope, a design that originated from Asmodeus himself. The fortress constructed from Baatorian green steel, and its inner halls were built from gold-veined marble bathed in ever-present golden light. Malsheem was the largest stronghold in all the Outer Planes, and considered among the mightiest in all of cosmology.

The city was constructed in the form of a colossal stalagmite, many miles wide and just as far tall, with a cross-shaped base that extended for miles along the depths of Nessus. A nearly infinite number of tunnels and passageways extended outward from Malsheem into the surrounding landscape, adjoining infernal garrisons and barracks for Asmodeus' army of devils.

An oppressive aura of dread permeated the entirety of Malsheem. While it was large enough to house millions upon millions of devils, some areas of the city were entirely uninhabited. These desolate halls held no notable landmarks, and were eerily silent. Even when no sounds were readily apparent, the faint cries of imprisoned souls could be heard as if in whisper.

Function
The city of Malsheem served as a meeting place for the Dark Eight, the generals that commanded the forces of the Hells in the Blood War.

Malsheem also served a second function as a repository for certain souls that had Asmodeus deemed noteworthy enough to hide away from others.

Geography
The city-spire of Malsheem was situated within a seemingly bottomless crevasse that split open the center of Nessus, where the Hell's Lips gorge gave way to Reaper's Canyon.

Rumors & Legends
It was rumored that Malsheem was to be the site of an infernal ritual known as the Bringing. During this rite, night hags would provide millions of soul larvae to the Dark Eight, which would subsequently be outright destroyed in one swoop. It was said this would grant the generals the ultimate power to destroy the tanar'ri once and for all.

Notable Locations
 Fortress Nessus, the desolate yet breathtakingly beautiful palace from which Asmodeus held court.

Inhabitants
The city was home to the thousands of devils that composed Asmodeus' army. Notable among these infernal shock troops was the legion of 1,001 brazen devils, armored guardians that sought no personal glory and only existed to serve the Lord of the Nine.

It was said that the iteration of Asmodeus encountered in Malsheem was merely his avatar, and the true Lord of the Nine dwelled deeper within Nessus.

## Mahaxara Khal

Mahaxara Khal was a human fighter and the Captain of the Royal Guard in service to Prince Andru of the Rock of Bral in the mid-to-late 14 century DR.

Description
She was tall and athletic of build. Mahaxara kept her head shaved bald but for a queue of long dark hair at the back, while tattoos of snakes covered both her arms, giving her what some considered a barbaric look.

Personality
She was a reticent warrior and, having no interest in the politics of the royal court, she commonly kept her thoughts to herself.

Abilities
Very difficult to take by surprise, Mahaxara had an almost superhuman alertness.

Possessions
Mahaxara wielded a +3 two-handed sword that she specialized in, but as back-up she also had a +2 short sword and a light crossbow with a half-dozen +3 bolts and three bolts of slaying, two dedicated to illithids and one to beholders. She wore +4 banded mail and a cloak of the bat. Finally, she had a potion of invisibility.

She had private quarters in Starhaven, the palace of Prince Andru in the High City of Bral. It was a spartan and spotlessly tidy place.

Relationships
She was a completely loyal to Prince Andru and House Cozar, and was never far from his side.

Mahaxara saw right through Lord Diadan Cartan's act as a witty fop and saw him for the vicious murderer he really was. In private, she hated the man and waited for the day she could confront him in a fair fight.

History
Hailing from some faraway world, Mahaxara Khal traveled on a spelljammer privateer before she arrived on the Rock of Bral. Already an experienced warrior, she enlisted in the Royal Guard and within eight years had risen to its command.

By the late 14 century DR, Maerae worked alongside Jalith at the Copper Coronet. Both women were paid only in food and drink. The Copper Coronet allowed them little time to make coin. The Man O' War had such a high reputation for elegance and safety that the rulers of Bral had visiting diplomats stay here when guestrooms in the Starhaven palace were fully occupied. Hallek was very respectful to guests.

There was a strict dress code in the dining room, and both weapons and armor were proscribed for patrons.

Security was provided by a force of elite mercenaries who were paid very well to guarantee guests' safety.

A standard dinner cost as much as 8–12 gp per person, but the food was top quality and the best in Bral, while the service was exceptional.

Moreover, it had ten luxurious suites of rooms that could be rented for 10–30 gp per night. This included breakfast each morning and a bottle of fine wine.

## Manriki

Manriki were a type of berry-bearing bush native to the Malatran Plateau of Kara-Tur.

Description
Manriki was a stout little flowering bush that was virtually indistinguishable from the biseechee shrub that bore edible berries. The only difference between the two species of plants was the manriki berries' deeper red color and three-petal flowers.

Properties
Despite being sweet and delicious, the berries of this plant were dangerously poisonous to most humanoids of the Living Jungle. Poisoning symptoms started with disorientation, biliousness, and a bad headache. If the affected individual started seeing spots, it was a telltale sign of incoming blindness that usually set in within a single hour after consumption. Thankfully, in most cases, blindness was not permanent and naturally passed within 3 to 30 minutes.

Curiously enough, manriki berry juice could be mixed with a secret concoction of a burning balm made of various jungle plants and substances. On its own, this type of burning balm was fairly weak, but with a small amount of manriki berry juice introduced into the mixture, the balm ignited with intense flames of orange, then yellow, then blinding white, hot enough to destroy some of the strongest magical obsidian items.

Availability
Just like biseechee, manriki grew on the fringes of the Rayanna Savannah of Malatra.

History
One year before the Year of Tigers Return, Malatran calendar, Bengoukee, a powerful witch doctor of the Tribe of Big Chief Bagoomba, prepared a burning balm in order to destroy a powerful artifact of evil corrupting power – Statue of K'lel'al. With his help, a band of heroes of the Living Jungle smothered the statue with the balm. With a single drop of manriki berry juice, the Statue of K'lel'al was no more.

## Mayastan Sadaar

She was insistent on traveling to the far-off city of Tashluta and learning more from the oracle of the House of the All-Seeing Orb, Valin Sarnaster. In fact, Mayastan sought to confront the oracle and prevent her from completing out the series of rituals outlined in the book.

One of Candlekeep's Great Readers, A'lai Aivenmore, became concerned at Mayastan's sudden shift in focus and set a group of adventurers to follow her to Tashluta.

Upon her arrival, Mayastan was received by the servants of Valin Sarnaster and taken into her inner sanctum. Mayastan's pancreas was forcibly removed and replaced with that of Valin Sarnaster, as part of the ritual that would transform the dragonborn sage into one of the oracle's canopic golems. Realizing the fate that awaited her after the transplant, Mayastan chose to end her own life and not allow Sarnaster to gain strength at the expense of her own body.

## Mark of brotherhood

Mark of brotherhood was a spell used by dwarven clerics.

Effects
When cast, a glyph appeared on each hand of the caster. One glyph was the symbol of the caster's clan, and the other the caster's holy symbol. The glyphs became invisible and were only visible to those dwarves who had the same glyphs. The glyphs were permanent, but they vanished if the caster committed a serious offense against their clan and/or clergy. If such a thing came to pass, the glyphs flared with a brilliant light and seared the caster's hands, causing them great pain and leaving behind scars. The scars were permanent; no amount of healing could remove them. The only way to remove the scars was if the caster made amends for their offenses.

Components
In addition to verbal and somatic components, this spell required as a material component a coin made from steel that had the caster's clan symbol on one side and their holy symbol on the other. The coin was consumed by the spell.

## Market Hall (Suzail)

The Market Hall was a galleria marketplace in the capital city of Suzail in Cormyr.

Location
The Market Hall stood at the southern end of the Coachwheels Way with the street forming a loop around the building. Directly north of the Market Hall were Six Coffers Trading Coster yards.

Visitors to Suzail were warned not to confuse the Market Hall to the east that dealt in produce with the western open-air market where merchants peddled clothing, tools, and other similar items.

The Market Hall was also known for its notice board, which often contained notices for the busy city's available lodgings.

Services
The Market Hall was the destination for greengrocers and farmers from outside of Suzail who brought their goods to be sold in the city. Fresh produce was carted to the Hall at the brink of dawn and purchased by locals and servants of wealthy households.

Apart from merchants, crafters, and other businesses within the Market Hall, stood a stone chair used to shame and punish miscreant shopkeepers. The guilds of Suzail did not tolerate unfair and low-quality merchant goods. The guilds-sponsored inspectors ensured the city's marketplaces ran reputable businesses. This scrutiny applied to traveling merchants from outside Suzail. Those caught swindling customers were chained to the stone chair in the Market Hall for an entire day with the defective goods on display for all to see. Rotten produced, and counterfeit alcohol was smeared all over the chain culprits.

## Mastermind

Masterminds were exceptionally cunning rogues that dealt in information and secrets over more tangible riches. Their careers were marked by lies, deceit, and most of all, intrigue.

Activities
These individuals often worked as royal courtiers or even spies, petitioning themselves among seats of power throughout the Realms in order to gain access to the most valuable information.

Culture
Due to their exceptional proficiency with managing social situations, masterminds were considered formidable opponents in the political landscape.

Possessions
Masterminds trained themselves in the use of disguise and forgery kits, in order to mask their identities and obfuscate their actions.

Abilities
These rogues studied hard to master numerous languages of the Realms and beyond. They even developed techniques to imitate foreign accents and individual speech patterns of others.

They were quick studies of character, and could glean useful information about someone through observation or a brief dialogue. Masterminds could rapidly assess the strengths or weaknesses of anyone's character in this manner.

While they were not the most fearsome combatants on their own, masterminds expertly assisted their allies in battle. By misdirecting their opponents, these rogues could redirect targeted attacks towards others nearby.

Expert masterminds honed their mental fortitude to the point where it could not be pierced by telepathy or other magical means, unless they so wished. Any lies or deceit they spread were similarly undetectable, unless they again wished otherwise.

## Many-Fanged Serpent

The Many-Fanged Serpent was a mercantile secret society that operated out of the town of Purskul in the Zehoarastria region of Amn, several centuries prior to the late 14 century DR.

History
The Many-Fanged Serpent held clandestine meetings in the Owlroost Head Inn of Purskul. Back then, the inn bore a different name, and the phrase "Owlroost Head", the name of a certain hill, was used as the secret society's password. The meetings of the Many-Fanged Serpent were attended by merchants and laborers and planned attacks against unjust treatment and price-gouging by the visiting traders, merchants, and corrupt rulers. These planned actions were often referred to as "Serpent striking."

As of the late 14 century DR, the Many-Fanged Serpent was presumed disbanded, but every time Purskul was shaken by vandalisms, mercantilism-related murders, or other trade disturbances, the locals attributed these acts to the Striking Serpent. The swearing "By the Serpent!" remained very common in Purskul.

It was believed that the largest dining hall of the Owlroost Head Inn was constructed atop a buried cache of money stolen by the Many-Fanged Serpent.

## Marketh

Lord Chamberlain Marketh was a thief and the administrative overseer of Dorn's Deep following its occupation by the allies of Revered Brother Poquelin during the late 13 century DR.

Personality
Marketh believed what he referred to as "New Dorn's Deep" would be a thriving community of Icewind Dale. He held a particular disdain for the dwarven people and did not allow them entrance into his burgeoning community.

He was wholly unethical individual who was not above resorting to barbarous means. He was also however an abject coward and would readily give in when he felt threatened.

Possessions
Marketh wore an suit of black dragon scale armor, and wielded two blades, the scimitar Valiant and an enchanted wakizashi. He was also in the possession of a ring of the gorgon.

Activities
He dwelled within a lavish palace in the lower depths of Dorn's Deep.

Relationships
According to Ilmadia Bariel, Marketh surrounded himself with friends that were idiotic louts.

History
Marketh was once part of an adventuring company that included a noble paladin, a wizard, and cleric, who together went to investigate Brother Poquelin and his activities in Icewind Dale. When the group confronted the Revered Brother, Poquelin offered them the opportunity to work for him. When Marketh's allies refused, he literally one of them in the back, as the others were dealt with by Poquelin.

As of the, Marketh remained loyal to Poquelin and watched over Dorn's Deep for his master. He was however, not truly devoted to the Revered Brother's cause.

## Mama Needs Her New Pair of Shu

Mama Needs Her New Pair of Shu is a tournament module set in Malatra – Living Jungle using the Dungeons & Dragons 2 edition ruleset. It is part of the Living Jungle series of adventures published for the RPGA Network,  and the third in the Shu series, following If the Shu Fits and The Soulless Shu adventures. It is intended for 1 through 5 Level characters.

Summary
In the Year of Great Change (1373 DR), two children of the Simbuki shu tribe were abducted by the dreaded servants of the Tamara – black leopard katanga. The children, named after the spirits of the jungle, Ekana, Huko, were to be consumed by akathasa. A group of heroes embarked on the rescue journey across the Rayanna Savanna, meeting a nature spirit Yato and a small army of Malatran mud-men, before confronting the leader of the leopard katanga – chief Many-Teeth.

## Majal

Majal's life tragically ended in her family's estate – Carlsmere, located on The Bite of the Dragon's Head Peninsula. During a dire storm, more than two hundred years before the, Prince Valys smothered his older brother, Prince Priam, along with royal children, Majal and her brother Vyshan. With the murders, Prince Valys ensured the crown was to be passed on to him from his great-grandfather Alemander I. However, Majal and her family's deaths were avenged by Priam's younger brother Coram III.

By the late 14 century, Carlsmere was an abandoned estate, still haunted by ghostly apparitions of those unjustly killed there. Rising Princess Majal and her brother could occasionally be heard or seen confusingly weeping and stumbling through the ruins and the manse's playhouse, seeking warmth and comfort in cold undead existence.

## Mantle (Cormathan)

The Cormathan mantle was a variation of the mantle popular in Cormanthyr.

Powers
The Cormathan version of a mantle was an intangible object about the shoulders, but which was centered in a gem. The mantle could store spells as attack, utility, or defensive ones; a defensive spell was always active, an attack spell could be used once daily, and an utility spell could be called upon up to thrice daily. These spells could be employed with an act of will, and did not require casting the spell, making them extremely flexible. However, any day in which the magic was called on, they spent a modest amount of lifeforce from their wearer.

Creation
The gem around which the mantle grew was to be steeped first in the caster's tears. Only the creator of a mantle could modify it, and with every additional spell put into the mantle, it significantly reduced their endurance in combat. The user could only add new spells into the mantle every time they reached new levels of proficiency with magic.

A number of hidden spells had been devised to grant the mantle other powers.

Known Users
The Coronal's mantle was unique in that it could call upon the power of his thrones, the Living Seat in the Isle of Estel and the Throne of the Coronal in the Chamber of the Court, as well as the Vault of the Ages or other sources of power if they were nearby.

Other known users were Cilivren Doedance and Nlaea.

Rumors & Legends
The wizard Malchor Harpell was assumed to be capable of creating a mantle from scratch.

The late witch Nunntchlea of Secomber was said to have hidden a spellbook somewhere in Waterdeep, and to have cast her own mantles ca. .

## Matrikay

Matrikay was a wizard-librarian as well as the proprietor of the Knowledge-Hold in Baldur's Gate during the late 15 century DR.

Personality
She held the preservation and sanctity of knowledge in the highest regard. While she would not necessarily put a friend in harm's way to learn more about the magical world, Matrikay would not turn down the opportunity if they happened to already escaped from peril.

Abilities
As a powerful wizard, Matrikay was capable of casting powerful spells, including among others private sanctum.

Activities
Matrikay specialized in the study of "eldritch lore", and spent much of her time researching wild magic.

Relationships

She was a friend of Delina a wild mage sorceress from Baldur's Gate who went on to have a prolific adventuring career. Matrikay and Delina worked together to better understand wild surges. They hoped to help Delina exert some manner of control over them, in order to make her less unpredictable spellcaster.

History
When Matrikay learned information about a place of "absolute order"―the plane of Mechanus―she used powerful magic to transport Delina there, with the hopes she could find a solution to her dangerous wild surges. Matrikay offered Delina a recall stone so that she could return safely, although there were some complications during her journey. The two we reunited at Knowledge-Hold after a short while, with Delina having gained much wisdom thanks to her friend's efforts.

Some time in the, Matrikay got into a series of heated disagreements with Knowledge-Hold's head librarian, Hayley Kroe. Kroe had been acting in bizarre ways over the course of a few days, and Matrikay suspected she was destroying unique, and seemingly irreplaceable documents. When Matrikay brought her concerns to Delina, the wild mage and her fellow adventurers agreed to investigate Knowledge-Hold. They discovered that Hayley Kroe had joined some mysterious cult, and that the Knowledge-Hold had been infiltrated by devotees of some entity known as the Absolute.

## Madachi Jhent

Madachi Jhent was a disgraced nobleman of Waterdeep who proclaimed himself the High Minister of Ao before being killed sometime before the late 14 century DR.

History
Madachi was an infamous individual in the City of Splendors whose story spread across Waterdeep like wildfire shortly after the Time of Troubles. He was a minor noble who lost all his wealth but delved into a delusion that convinced him to lead the new church after seeing a vision of Ao, the High God of Toril in his cloak. He started his preaching career proselytizing to a pen of pigs and pronounced damnations on sinners who resided in a bowl of soup. Madachi's infamy came after he started preaching gibberish to a group of poor Waterdhavians who eventually became agitated. The High Minister kicked a homeless man in the face and that act somehow cured the poor wretch's blindness (as the penniless noble was wearing enchanted boots later known as A Mad Gent's Boots). This miraculous deed attracted a gaggle of followers to the so-called "High Minister." New auditions to Madachi's church lacked the fire of insanity that ignited the "High Minister's" passionate Kicking Crusade across Waterdeep.

Miraculously, Madachi Jhent's kicks did not cause the crazed minister's demise, as his followers valiantly protected him. Eventually, as the Kicking Crusade continued, minister Jhent realized his kicks did no miracles as the victims of his kicks were not suffering from illness. However, another "miracle" was taking place. As Madachi helped his victims up from the streets, his gloves, later known as A Mad Gent's Gloves, cured those he touched. This attracted yet another wave of followers to the misguided church.

The High Minister of Ao spent several next days touching people after kicking them, spreading the healing "miracle." But his foolish luck ended when he kicked a grimly-armored cleric of Bane in the face. The cleric was a follower of then the dead god of hatred and tyranny and retaliated by throttling the dimwitted miracle dispenser. Madachi demanded to be unhanded because "no servant of a dead god is fit to touch a servant of Ao." Despite not having divine magics at his disposal, the priest of Bane handled the "High Minister" and his gaggle of lunatics with ease.

## Mage-killer

Mage-killers were rare individuals who mastered the use of combat magic specifically to be used against other spellcasters.

Culture
These individuals were often bounty hunters who specialized in tracking down and capturing, or slaying, mages. Followers of both Azuth and Shar often hired them for jobs. Azuth's faithful used mage-killers as a last resort against a mage who continually ignored their condemnation of their abuse of magic. Shar's faithful usually had a mage-killer execute a target in a public manner to send a grisly message and weaken Mystra's hold on the Weave.

Abilities
Mage-killers often developed martial skills designed to be effective against magic-users. They could cast spells used by wizards and priests. Mage-killers possessed an assortment of skills allowing them to gather information on their targets and hunt them without being discovered. Given their extensive knowledge of the spells they used to attack others, mage-killers stood a better chance of resisting the effects if the same spells were used against them.

Possessions
They typically carried a variety of equipment similar to normal bounty hunters.

## Malachlabra

Malachlabra was an archfiend and the daughter of Dispater in the late 14 century DR. She was ambushed by the Simbul in .

Description
Malachlabra was humanoid in form, with comely features and a lush body as black as obsidian. She had fingers ending in talons the length of a man's arm, sleek bat wings ruby red on the outside and black on the inside, and three snake tails, at least one of which ended in a glossy black spade-shape.

Her horned head sat upon her unnaturally long neck. Behind her red, beautiful lips was a forked tongue, while a flame burned at the back of her ale-brown eyes.

Abilities
She could cast or use a sphere of seeing, which allowed her to scry, but it failed when brought to look at its own environment. She was also capable of some amount of short-range teleportation, and of throwing her consciousness into even the least object to escape her own death. The spade-shape at her tail end was sharp enough to slash while being whipped.

She had the ability to contact another person's mind, and was confident of her ability to remove other archdevils' influence from humans' minds. She could also spit fire.

Relationships
Malachlabra claimed to be the daughter of Dispater. She considered Nergal a brute.

History
At some point, she had slain a dragon for its lair. In the, she briefly came across Elminster Aumar while he was being tormented by Nergal. Though she volunteered to free the old wizard from Nergal's mental influence, she was bested by him.

Soon afterwards the Simbul stormed Avernus trying to rescue Elminster. Nergal had transformed Elminster and hid him in Malachlabra's lair, luring the Simbul towards his rival; the Simbul quickly ambushed and destroyed Malachlabra, who just barely survived by hiding her sapience in a spark and fleeing. She survived, barely.

## Ma'at

Ma'at was the uniting, arguably overgod principle of the Mulhorandi and Pharaonic pantheons. The exact meaning was not easily understood, but it combined features of many concepts of ethics into one overarching code of conduct. However, Ma'at was far more than a simple behavioral standard, but revered as the natural, divine, and fundamental state of all reality.

All things were expected to conform to Ma'at, for it put the gods, pharaohs, and commoners in their rightful place and allowed for peace between mortals and gods. To follow it was the one path to a happy life and to refuse could only be expected to result in misery and turmoil. Allegedly, without Ma'at, the very existence of the gods would be without foundation and the universe would crumble.

For lack of better terms, Ma'at could be treated as the natural desire of all persons to live a lawful good life. Its composite concepts might best be described as truth, integrity, honor, duty, order, constancy, justice, and righteousness. Following Ma'at meant fulfilling one's moral obligations to others, and applied to those of high station as much as those of low. Just as the common citizens were expected to put in an honest day's work and follow the law, so too was the ruler expected to provide compensation and administrate with fairness.

Notable Adherents
Most deities of the Pharaonic pantheon praised and upheld Ma'at as the underpinning order of their divine being and the Mulhorandi dynasty were heirs to its maintenance.

Horus-Re was a strong believer in Ma'at. According to his doctrine, harmony came from living within it rather than fighting it. The laws existed to bring prosperity to its followers and the pharaoh and his representatives set laws as guidelines for honorable and traditional behavior. Should the guidelines not be applied with honor, however, Osiris's fair judgement was left to determine the law.

Outside the Mulhorandi pantheon, Anubis weighed the souls of deceased mortals against the feather of Ma'at, revealing them to be just and honorable and worthy of reward should his scale balance, or else be fed to a devourer of souls if it tipped the scale.

Mortal judges who followed Ma'at invoked its presence so as to decide cases with impartial justice. Similarly, rulers strove to govern according to the principles of Ma'at so justice and order would mark their rule, often seeking advice from clerics to do so.

Notable Detractors
While all deities in the Pharaonic pantheon at the very least showed respect or keen interest in Ma'at, Apep, Sebek, and Set did not hold it in high regard. Apep was a being of primordial chaos banished by the pantheon and Set, despite being willing to side with his pantheon against Apep, was opposed to Ma'at by his nature.

Disrupting Ma'at
The Pharaonic pantheon was concerned more about the fight of law against chaos (though they did espouse free choice and individuality) than of good against evil. They counted their true foes not the simply malicious, but those who would destroy and send humanity back to their primitive origins. By Horus-Re's interpretation, that which led to evil was by its nature unlawful, and that which caused chaos unnatural. Treachery and traitors were similarly not to be abided, for such dishonorable behavior was against the divine order. Disrespecting the dead, such as by despoiling their resting places, was a violation of Ma'at particularly hated by Osiris.

## Magdar Shenlen

Most ship captains knew the man and expected him to show up immediately on their arrival. However, in the, Magdar failed to appear as the Wicked Wench docked, carrying mercenary adventurers from the city of Luskan to the south. Captain Hedron Kerdos smelled trouble and he was right. An army of Legion of the Chimera goblins found a way into the docks of Targos and were wreaking havoc.

Magdar retreated to one of the warehouses just off the docks and locked himself inside, surrounded by goods belonging to the Gallaway Coster. Eventually, his hiding spot was discovered by the adventurers from Luskan, with a band of goblins following them into the warehouse and attacking. He underestimated the power of the dust, and the resulting backlash nearly killed Roderio, drenching him in caustic acid and shredding him with shards of glass. Her quick thinking and readiness helped save Roderio's life when Keph caused his workshop to explode, treating him with potions of healing until a cleric healer could arrive.

After the festivities, it appeared that Lord Thistle had been murdered by extraordinary means, but the Magebane's aversion to using spells or magical items made them an unlikely culprits.

## Mad Berfy

Mad Berfy was a gnome adventurer and member of the Emerald Swords company circa 1369 DR, who specialized as an illusionist wizard.

Description
Berfy had a bright blue mohawk, and seemed to be unable to stop giggling.

Personality
Mad Berfy was appropriately eccentric in his behaviour, and annoyed his companions with his quirky tendencies.

Abilities
He was a skilled illusionist, and knew an array of spells that confused or misled his enemies.

Possessions
Berfy carried a dagger and a wand of illusion, and wore a cloak of displacement.

History
In 1369 DR, Mad Berfy and the Emerald Swords were guests at Thistleflame Keep in Suzail. They conspired to kidnap Lord Partic Thistle and hand him over to Zhentil Keep for questioning, and had Xixis the doppelganger impersonate Lord Thistle to allow them to escape without suspicion. When Xixis risked carelessly ruining the plan, Gandegar Armstrong had Haridyn Storm kill Xixis with a dagger of venom, so that the Lord's murder would cover up his kidnapping. Despite their best attempts at diversion, the Emerald Swords were caught and Lord Thistle rescued. For their murder and kidnapping, they risked exile or execution for their crimes.

## Marlamin

Marlamin was a halfling inhabitant of Longsaddle in the Savage Frontier in the late 15 century DR.

Description
With a bright and friendly manner, he had wavy brown hair and a short grey-peppered beard. He tended to wear a plain shirt, vest, and pants.

Abilities
His hobbies included prettying up his cottage, working in the garden, writing a book, and learning to play the panpipes.

Relationships

Marlamin was the husband of first Holga Kilgore, whom he divorced, and then Gwinn. He had loving relationships with them, but had not been able to bear the fear for Holga's safety and freedom. Generally, he appeared to have a particular attraction to barbarian human women.

History
Marlamin met and fell in love with Holga Kilgore, an Uthgardt human barbarian of the Elk tribe. However, because he was outsider, Holga was kicked out of her Elk tribe and shunned. Holga and Marlamin married regardless.

Once, while in the Greypeak Mountains, Holga stole what she thought was a mere walking stick from a wizard she'd encountered and gifted it to Marlamin.

However, their marriage later fell apart. Holga could not let go of the pain of her banishment, for all of Marlamin's efforts to make her a new home, and he was sick of fearing for her safety and whereabouts, given her life of crime, and often wept late into the night. Finally, he separated from her. Rootless in the world, Holga wandered for a while as she sought new bonds and eventually wound up in Targos in Icewind Dale, where she fell in with Edgin Darvis.

Later, Marlamin sent Holga a letter stating he was no longer her husband and formally their ending their marriage. Nevertheless, she still held feelings for Marlamin, considering him "one of the finest men in Faerûn". After she and Edgin escaped from Revel's End prison in the late 1490s DR, she wanted to visit Marlamin for closure.

Meanwhile, Marlamin had met and married another barbarian woman, Gwinn. They'd been together almost a year when Holga visited. Marlamin explained he preferred that Gwinn made an honest living, not thieving. They shared their reasons for their past struggles and separation. Accepting that Marlamin was happy with Gwinn, Holga departed, taking with her the old walking stick she'd once given him and thinking he looked even better than she recalled. Later, the couple had a goose and pickleberries for dinner.

Appendix
Background
Marlamin is played by actor Bradley Cooper in an uncredited cameo. However, before the movie's release, Dexter Fletcher stated in an early interview that he played the same role. It's possible that Fletcher only appeared as a stand-in to give Michelle Rodriguez someone to act against. It was confirmed in a later interview, here, that Cooper was introduced via CGI later, with Rodriguez unaware of his part until afterward. A child actor was also used as a stand-in, as revealed by Jonathan Goldstein here.

Scenes outside Marlamin's cottage were filmed on location in the abandoned village of Galboly in Northern Ireland. The exterior cottage set was originally built for Game of Thrones and was remodeled with new door-frame pillars and door, windows, added thatch and moss on the roof, and a chimney, with gardens and farms created around it.

## Mageripper

Magerippers were tiny, utterly bizarre aberrations that both sensed and fed on magic, much to the detriment of any spellcasters in their vicinity.

Description
On average, adult magerippers were only  long and weighed . They were eyeless, and instead had circular discolorations marking the location of specialized magic-sensing organs. The legs were insect-like, the two tentacles vaguely like those of a displacer beast, and the body was conical with oversized, sharp-toothed jaws. Magerippers were sickly purple, blue, and/or pink in color.

Behavior
Magerippers were animalistic, solely concerned with finding food and breeding. They weren't intentionally destructive but they were highly erratic.

Abilities
Magerippers were blind, but they could innately sense any magic auras within  of the swarm, and just as naturally could detect the strength and nature of the auras, as well as any use of spells or spell-like abilities. When the swarm entered the same space, it could feed on an ongoing spell or spell-like effect, effectively dispelling it. More passively, magerippers swarms drained magic out of other creatures, reducing their magical abilities over time.

Combat
Mageripper swarms were relentless in pursuit of food, always heading for the strongest magic aura they could sense and surrounded the source until it was drained or destroyed.

Ecology
Magerippers lived in temperate climates and were drawn to places with strong and plentiful sources of magical energy, typically urban areas or regions home to many fey and/or elves. Beings inimical to magic were known to try and encourage magerippers to settle in their area, but the creatures, while effective guardians, were prone to leaving in search of more magiferous feeding grounds; other uses included using them as a defense against magical assaults. "Keepers" of swarms were known to cast a spell on a captive, or binding a spellcaster, and leave them to be killed by the hungry swarm.

Technically, magerippers could survive by eating meat, but they thrived on magical energy and required it to reproduce. Magerippers
reproduced via asexual budding. With enough magic, a swarm could double its numbers within days; in such instances the swarm split into two that went their separate ways. Individual magerippers only lived one year, and grew sluggish, unresponsive, and eventually dead if separated from their swarm.

They could not feed on the magic in magical items, but still swarmed around such treasures.

Mageripper swarms were among the creatures found in the sewers of Waterdeep, and they had also been reported living in Skullport. Additionally, the Thayan enclaves established by the Red Wizards often contained many magic items, making such places magnets for mageripper swarms, and keeping the swarms under control was a constant concern of the Thayans.

History
Mageripper swarms were so bizarre that most scholars theorized that they had been deliberately created for some unknown purpose.

## Manual of puissant skill at arms

A manual of puissant skill at arms was a powerful magical tome that could instil great wisdom and experience in a warrior.

Powers
A fighter or bard that studied the manual for one month not only benefited from its in-depth accounts of fighting styles, but was magically instilled with the experience they needed to take their martial skills to the next level and then some. They could not benefit from reading the manual a second time.

Rangers and paladins were able to read the contents, but did not magically benefit from the magical power of the manual. Clerics and rogues found the book completely incomprehensible, and a wizard who dared scan its pages found themselves stunned and reeling as their arcane experiences were torn from them.

History
 The book-collecting lich Adzerak held a manual in his library collection at Barrenstone.

A manual of stealthy pilfering was a powerful magical tome that could take a thief to new heights of ability.

Description
Manuals of stealthy pilfering were bound in black hide.

Powers
A rogue or bard who read the manual found that the text disappeared after reading, but if they practiced the skills detailed within for one month they were magically instilled with the experience they needed to take their sneaking, pilfering, and skulduggery skills to the next level and then a bit further. They could not benefit from reading the manual a second time.

Fighters and wizardss were unable to understand a word of the manual. Clerics, paladins and rangers who dared steal a glance at the contents found their minds assailed with damaging concepts, stunned and helpless as their high-handed experiences melted away. If they did not receive an atonement within a day, they also suffered a permanent damage to their common-sense and judgment.

 The book-collecting lich Adzerak held a manual in his library collection at Barrenstone. Another copy belonged to white dragon Lokelis Brightburn, who laired in a cave near the Haunted Halls of Eveningstar in the 15 century DR.

## Mae

Mae was the proprietor of the Friendly Bat tavern in the village of Womford during the late 15 century DR. She originally ran the tavern-and-inn with her husband Grunnald, but then took over sole proprietorship after he "went missing" under mysterious circumstances.

Personality
She was a strong woman who was determined to run her business in spite of several hardships.

Relationships

Mae was a devoted wife to Grunnald. After his supposed death, she made a loving, if somewhat disturbing, effigy of him, which she proudly displayed in the Friendly Bat's taproom. The two had one daughter, a sweet but clumsy girl named Muren.

History

Sometime during the 1490s DR, the local gang known as the Pale Claw took over the town of Womford and began extorting its citizens. Unbeknownst to Mae, her husband Grunnald faked his own death, and joined the gang as their "Bandit King", helping redirect their crimes towards people beyond the village. Mae was wholly unaware of her husband's misguided attempt to right their wrongs, and mourned her family's loss deeply.

Mae and Muren tried to make ends meet by continuing keep the Friendly Bat open in Womford. They made little in the way of income however, as the Pale Claw resumed its extortion racket over the town's people. Their fortune changed however, when a band of adventurers, namely Edgin Darvis, Holga Kilgore, Simon Aumar, Forge Fitzwilliam, and Thelvyn Kip, came through town. With the few precious silver she had left, Mae hired the adventurers to rid Womford of the Pale Claw once and for all.

While somewhat bumbling in their efforts, the adventurers managed to successfully disrupt the bandit gang's operations, and force them to find better prospects elsewhere. They even managed to uncover Grunnald's ruse, and gave him the opportunity to return home. The reunion was a wondrous event at first, before turning south. While Mae seemed embittered about the whole situation, she received one last boon as patron of the adventuring party: a porcelain boar figure filled with gold coins and gems.

## Magic-suppression cuff

Magic-suppression cuffs were bracelets or manacles that prevented the wearer from casting spells or using other magical abilities.

Description
Magic-suppression cuffs were worn loosely about the wrist, and consisted of two overlapping loops of golden metal that met at a lock. A cuff was locked or unlocked with a key.

Powers
Anyone who wore a magic-suppression cuff was unable to call upon their magical abilities, including spellcasting or powers such as wild shape. Only a single cuff on one wrist was necessary to subdue the magic of even a mighty wizard. It was not necessary that the cuff be secured tightly to take effect.

History
When the High Sun Games were revived in Neverwinter during the late 1490s DR, magic-suppression cuffs were placed on spellcasting participants to prevent them from using magic to survive the Games. A collection of such cuffs, along with their keys, was maintained in a storage area beneath Neverwinter arena.

As part of the Games, a group of adventurers and thieves—Edgin Darvis, Holga Kilgore, Simon Aumar, and Doric—were sent into the Games to die by Lord Forge Fitzwilliam and the Red Wizard Sofina. Magic-suppression cuffs were placed on both the sorcerer Simon and the druid Doric, who confirmed that they were unable to use their magical abilities while wearing them. However, Doric was able to lose her cuff after her arm became stuck in a gelatinous cube, and the loose-fitting manacle came off when she pulled out her arm. Subsequently, the party escaped beneath the Arena and found the keys to remove Simon's cuff. When they later fought the powerful Sofina, the party only managed to win by deceiving her into letting down her guard so that Edgin's daughter, Kira, could sneak up using her pendant of invisibility and affix Simon's magic-suppression cuff onto Sofina's wrist.

## Mauletar

Mauletar was a guardsman from the nation of Thay who became the namesake of the battle axe of Mauletar in the 11 century DR.

History
In the, the Red Wizard nation of Thay became consumed by a short but bloody civil war when the people of the nation rose against the Zulkirs. During the war, Mauletar escorted members of the House Ormynd out of the war-torn nation. He had befriended the family and wanted them to reach safety. As they fled, it became apparent that the family was betrayed. Mauletar picked up Ormynd's enchanted axe and stood against the family's enemies, allowing them to flee to safety. Mauletar's battle cry shook the land before being snuffed out. His death was not forgotten. The axe he wielded became known as the battle axe of Mauletar, and his name became the symbol of loyalty and devoted friendship.

## Maxoris

Maxoris was a spice and preservative that originated in the Eastern Heartlands town of Proskur.

Description
Maxoris was a white powder that was used by a caravan company from Proskur to preserve fresh meat for many weeks, which was a much longer-lasting method compared to salt and other spices. The main disadvantage of maxoris was the strong musty taste it imparted to meat, overriding any other taste it might have and causing severe revulsion in some people. It found some popularity outside of Proskur among travelers and explorers who wanted to have fresh meat on hand and didn't mind the taste, especially those who explored the far North where the severe cold made taste irrelevant.

Availability
Maxoris was made from the seed of the maxor plant, which grew along the lower Tun River near the southern Storm Horns and Proskur. It grew to shoulder height and had long, drooping, fern-like leaves. The seeds were contained in a bulb at the top of the plant, with ten plants having enough to pack and preserve a  of meat.

## Macklin Talctuft

Macklin Talctuft was a dwarf who settled in Phandalin during the late 15 century DR.

Description
They had a beard and a mohawk-style hair cut.

Personality
Macklin had a general disinterest in tradition. They also abhorred doing anything that they found boring, and sought out work opportunities that would engage their creativity. Once they found such an opportunity, they were reliable and enthusiastic as they tackled their duties. However, they also had perfectionist tendencies, which could irritate coworkers or subordinates who found them to be impossible to please.

Activities
Macklin was a wanderer who performed odd jobs around Phandalin, but was content to remain unemployed when they found such work too boring.

History
While still young by dwarven standards, Macklin arrived in Phandalin sometime after its resettlement in the late 15 century DR looking for work in the mines. When they discovered that there was little mining to be done, they turned to odd jobs before electing to live off their savings while looking for work that would inspire them.

By the, they planned to join the Fellowship of the Golden Mongoose, a franchise of Acquisitions Incorporated that had recently arrived in Phandalin, however this plan was derailed when the Fellowship was mysteriously wiped out by an explosion that also badly damaged the ruins of Tresendar Manor. The prospect of rebuilding the Manor soon captured Macklin's imagination, leading them to offer their services to oversee a reconstruction project.

## Magnus Cadorna

Magnus Cadorna was the member of the textile merchant House Cadorna who brought the family to prominence over four generations before the mid-14 century DR.

History
Back when the Cadorna clan lived in obscurity, the family seamster business suffered greatly when their home and its surrounding lands became plagued by a red dragon. The family's eldest son, Magnus Cadorna, joined the local militia assembled to fight the winged wyrm, or at least to control and minimize the red menace's ransacking. Eventually, adventurers flocked to slay the dragon, and the militia waited in reserve. Unsurprisingly, the adventurers failed, but not before the dragon was wounded. Enraged, the wyrm decided to rain fire on the village that aided the adventurers. Most of the militia was slain by the dragon; Magnus Cadorna was the only man standing, desperate and badly hurt. The man managed to drive the dragon back and finished the dragon off with a fatal blow.

The feat made Magnus Cadorna a hero of the Dragon Reach, and his family received money and accolades that elevated the Cadorna clan to a position of power. Soon enough, members of the now greatly respected Cadorna family spread across the Dragon Reach region, forming a profitable textile trading company.

On the fifteenth anniversary of the dragon's death, the comparative Cadorna family sword was forged and presented to Magnus, now an eighty-two years old man. He was thankful but considered the gesture to be silly. The blade would remain with the Cadorna family, passed from father to son for four generations until it eventually left the "dragon killer" family's possession.

## Mattis

Mattis was a young entrepreneur who was among the tieflings exiled from the city of Elturel in the late 15 century DR. He was described as a 'collector of valuable objects', which were in fact mostly useless.

Description
Mattis had short gray-brown hair cut just above shoulder length. He dressed in a simple leather vest, blue trousers, and wore a notable amulet around his neck.

Personality
He had a knack for attracting and catching the attention of prospective customers. He used a combination of flattery and sleight of hand to keep people engaged and interested in viewing his wares.

Activities
Mattis was one of the numerous tiefling children who worked for the aspiring criminal mastermind Mol. Mattis' role in the gang was that of a friendly face to passersby. He sold all manner of items and trinkets, of varying degrees of usefulness, from food and tools to books and fantastical jewelry that purportedly granted significant powers.

Possessions
Mattis shop included numerous mundane items that could be of some use to others, including some food, a shovel, a set of thieves' tools, kitchen utensils, and even a starfish. More interesting however were the "magic" pieces of jewelry he had for sale. Notable among these were the ring of being really invisible, a ring of the lekinesus, attached to which was a small bit of fishing line tied to a rock, a ring of resistance to ants, which was adorned with a drop of sap containing several dead ants, and the ring of infinite wishes, which was inscribed with completely nonsensical runes.

He also offered for sale a copy of Tarbell's Guide to Distractions and a single arrow of Ilmater.

History
In the, every tiefling in Elturel was exiled from the city, following the catastrophic event in which the city was pulled down to the Nine Hells for a short time. Mattis and other children were among the refugees that followed the Hellrider officer Zevlor, en route to the great city of Baldur's Gate to the west.

It was during that journey that Mattis and other tiefling children began to work with Mol, the aspiring future criminal overlord of Baldur's Gate. When the tiefling refugees settled om the Emerald Grove for a time, Mol, Mattis, and others formed a little hideaway in a secluded area of the grove.

## Magic of the Weave

Magic of the Weave was an academic work that described the nature of the Weave, its association with magic, historical events, and other phenomena.

Content
An Introduction
The introduction to Magic of the Weave outlined the nature of the Weave, describing it as an "essential element" of existence that allowed individuals to access various forms of magic. It was not magic itself, but a tapestry of substance that could be manipulated by spellcasters.

It discussed  the different ways in which casters could access the Weave, through inherent connections formed at birth, years of study and practice, or deals for power made with entities beyond Toril.

Mystra and the Spellplague
This chapter of the book shared how Mystra, the goddess of magic, was herself the Weave.

History
As of the, there remained a copy of Magic of the Weave in the libraries of the Emerald Grove.

## Maris Khorma Terrabin

Maris Khorma Terrabin was a wizard, explorer, adventurer, and ecologist who traveled the Realms widely in the 14 century DR and studied the people, places and creatures in it.

Personality
Maris was rather proud of her deep knowledge of the lands she had explored, as well as her abilities as a wizard.

She was very critical of goblins in particular, holding them to generally be cruel, cowardly, and foolish looters and raiders.

History
Maris grew up in the tame and well-ordered lands of central Cormyr, and apprenticed under the wizard Felbour. She became enamored with tales of monsters and ruins, and at the first opportunity joined a company of adventurers on a jaunt through the Stonelands in search of the legendary Citadel of Seligonil. They ventured for months in the region, fighting border raiders and monsters, and though they did not find the mythical Citadel, Maris gained an abiding appreciation for the mysteries and treasures of the Stonelands.

She and her companions built a wooden keep in the just north of the High Moors, and used it as a base to further explore the Stonelands, Goblin Marches, Thunder Peaks, Storm Horns, Farsea Marshes, Skull Gorge, and into Anauroch in search of Rasilith. In later years, her companions perished or drifted apart, and she moved on to new adventures in the west, pausing briefly in the 1360s DR to write a regional guide for her friend Elminster.

## Margrath's Rest

Margrath's Rest was a rocky beach west of Suzail used as a ship graveyard, named for an old naval captain called Margrath who spent his retirement on the shore there.

Description
Decades after it stopped being used, the rocky coast was still home to several prominent wrecks inhabited by a profusion of eels and clams that found homes in the underwater hulks.

History
Before the reign of King Azoun IV, the beach was used for the disposal of large, decrepit ships that couldn't be effectively handled at sea. The ships were ran aground onto the shore and stripped of any valuable or useful fittings, with the timbers left to rot. The beach eventually fell out of use, but during the 14 century DR it was still home to many rotted hulks.

## Malaria

Malaria was an insect-transmitted disease, common in swamps and wetlands.

Acquisition
Mosquitoes, ants of the Kebi Swamp, and stirges were among the most common carriers of the disease. Malaria was a seasonal disease in the lands of Kara-Tur. Kozakura's city Jitogawa's Foreign Ward was built by the Shibi Swamp and every summer, several swamp-born afflictions like malaria and cholera washed over it. Some waters in Zakhara were known to harbor malaria.

Swamp druids were immune to diseases transmitted by insects, including malaria.

Treatment
Halflings of Luiren learned a special skill of medicinal cooking that involved making foods using Luiren spring cheese. Apprentice cooks knew how to prepare meals that could cure many diseases, including malaria.

History
Sometime before the, Golodon the Unmanned died from a severe case of malaria, complicated by a fireball spell being pushed down his throat by his nemesis named Dradu or Dradeen, according to Jan Jansen.

## Maskyr's Tower

Maskyr's Tower was a ruined mage's tower in the vale of Maskyr's Eye in the Vast. It was built by the archmage known as Maskyr One-Eye in the 7 century DR. Although since destroyed, it still held many mysteries.

Location
Before its obliteration, the tower stood on a rocky bluff that rose above the trees around Maskyr's Eye, roughly due south of the village center and on the west of the road. Further south was Hulvesper Farm. This bluff resembled the prow of a ship and pointed northeast toward the Coldstars, a pair of twin peaks in the Earthspur Mountains. This high bluff gave one a commanding view of the valley and the North Road, so watchposts were established here by visiting Mulmasterite riders on two occasions when orc hordes were feared in the region.

Structure
While it still stood, the tower was known to be small, rugged, and lacking embellishments. By the mid–14 century DR, however, there wasn't much left apart from the rubble lying about the place, grown over with shrubs and long grass. Much of the surviving stonework had been robbed out by the villagers of Maskyr's Eye for reuse in their cottages and walls. Nevertheless, the site was still an unnerving place at nights.

Defenses
Maskyr placed wards of force over the tower's door and windows, and these remained even after his disappearance, barring all entry.

History
Intact
After giving his right eye for the vale in payment to Deep King Tuir Stonebeard of the dwarven realm of Roldilar in the, Maskyr then went and dwelled there erecting the tower that came to bear his name for his home.

Others followed, and this marked the beginning of permanent human settlement in the Vast. A small settlement soon arose in the vale. Maskyr, meanwhile, lived peacefully and alone in his tower in his vale for several centuries. Finally, he went on a journey to the planes and disappeared, and was presumed to have been slain. However, some sages theorized that Maskyr had eventually moved out as people settled in his vale, leaving his old tower as a trap while he moved into the Mage's Tower on the other side of the Flooded Forest. Elminster declared this to be false, however.

Destruction
Over time, a number of ex-adventurers retired to the vale, and occasionally they went to Maskyr's Tower to try their luck on its wards, thinking they might find some heretofore undiscovered vulnerability. Yet its wards proved impenetrable, so they left with nothing. Eventually, one retired adventurer of Maskyr's Eye named Gathen Swiftsword resolved to take a brute-force approach. He rode to Mulmaster and returned with a 30-strong crew of hired 'strongarm' laborers whom he ordered to simply tunnel through the walls with bars, hammers, and picks. After two days of effort, they'd made one breach and almost had a second. Impatient to begin, the Swiftsword donned his old armor and collected his old weapons, and headed inside. He would never return.It is unknown when these events occur, but given that Khonduil is still alive as of the late 1350s DR, it is presumed to be within his lifetime and thus somewhere in the late 13 century to early 14 centuries DR.

The workers, who'd remained outside to widen the breach, later reported glimpsing inside "shifting shadows" and hearing, as one described, "odd, high calls, like a bird or bells, high and far-off?" They knew nothing of what transpired within. But following close behind Gathen was the thief Khonduil Ammargath, going unseen thanks to a potion of invisibility. It would save his life too. In an upper level, Gathen encountered a gargoyle-like guardian monster that proceeded to rip his arms and legs off. Khonduil used the distraction to creep by and he claimed a wizard's staff and a wand. As the guardian finished with Gathen and began to hunt for new prey, Khonduil pointed the wand and spoke the command word conveniently inscribed on its handle. The guardian enlarged and changed, transforming into a mighty dragon so massive the tower exploded around it, causing stones to rain down around the site at the start of dusk of that day. With a triumphant roar, the dragon spread wings as wide as the tower was high, and flew off to the north as the tower collapsed. Witnesses disagreed on its kind, on whether its scales were brassy, or green, or white, or even like electrum. Whatever it was, Khonduil would believe it to be the thing's true form.

Come morning, people returned warily to the site to survey the ruins, finding only a circle of fallen stones, no furnishings or treasures, and certainly nothing living. One farmer, Udzgul Thairharrow, claimed to have spotted a silvery doorway appearing for an instant in the air high over the ruins at sunset, but no-one believed him because they thought him a half-wit. Some others reported the same thing later, but they too were dismissed. Soon after the collapse, the Mulmasterite laborers began to turn over the stones, but when they heard digging noises coming from underground, noises that gradually got louder, most of them lost what was left of their nerves and fled. The remainder started to excavate and discovered a deep shaft; finding it held water, they decided it was simply a well.

Meanwhile, the thief Khonduil had survived his fall from the falling tower. He lost the wand, but kept hold of the staff. At some point, when he recovered, the tower was gone and the surprised strongarms were in their camp, so he crept away to seek his fortune some place much more peaceful.It's unclear when this occurred, but it's possible that Khonduil was the one digging his way out.

Ruins
In later days, dwarves came to survey the ruins. Then, predictably, treasure hunters descended on the site, mostly adventurers and lone young mages, and some caused trouble by threatening or enchanting the villagers for information, thinking they'd surely stolen and hidden the treasures of Maskyr's Tower.

One day, another mage, one Loathren of Phlan, came to Maskyr's Eye and made efforts to erect a new tower on the place where Maskyr's Tower had once stood, perhaps in an attempt to learn the old archmage's secrets and magic. However, the stones laying about the bluff rose up of their own accord, spun about like leaves in a whirlwind, and rained down upon his camp, killing Loathren. Naturally, stories spread that this was Maskyr One-Eye's doing, or his abandoned magic, or a curse. Yet others claimed the local dwarves were responsible, somehow, or that it was the work of a rival wizard opposed to Loathren acquiring Maskyr's arcane mastery. The curse story proved more popular and bards carried it far, so much fewer adventurers and ambitious mages came poking around the site.

In time, the folk of Maskyr's Vale took much of the stones away in their carts, and nature began to reclaim the remaining rubble.

Reputation
Believing it best not to disturb the doings of long-dead wizards, the folk of Maskyr's Vale were quick to warn travelers not to set foot there, given its history. Nevertheless, some reckless sorts did camp amongst the ruins overnight and would light a fire there.

Rumors & Legends
Local tales maintained Maskyr had had much treasure and mighty magic and that it could still be concealed somewhere nearby his old tower. Yet there was also a warning, that Maskyr the One-Eyed would someday return and hunt down all those who had taken from him, even a single copper piece.

Either way, regardless of all the searches and destruction, no treasure had ever been uncovered by anyone by the late 1350s DR, not unless they'd discovered and taken it away in secret and never said a word about their wins. Nevertheless, old Khonduil, who'd returned to Maskyr's Vale as a cleric of Tymora, was a believer in the treasure tale, thinking much of it was yet to be found. He supposed the silver door seen in the sky was a permanent portal or gate, leading anywhere from a cavern under the bluff to a far-flung corner of Faerûn, or even another plane. Once a door or wall in Maskyr's Tower, maybe hidden behind a tapestry, it would now be suspended unseen high in the air and out of reach. Curious to know the truth, but unwilling to risk life and limb again, he spoke often about the tales of Maskyr One-Eye and his treasure with minstrels, travelers, and villagers, but never gave any hint of his past or personal involvement.

## Marilyn Mittlemer

Marilyn Mittlemer was the wife of Mortimer Mittlemer, an illusionist con-artist from Ravens Bluff, the Living City in the mid-14 century DR.

Abilities
She was an accomplished thief who approached her carefully selected marks with utmost caution.

Relationships
Mortimer was a deeply selfish and greedy man. He married Marilyn because he wanted to use her thieving skills, but despite that, he did eventually fall in love with the woman. Despite being married, Mortimer claimed 60% of their loot, and Marilyn got only 30% of the take. Marilyn, however, adored her husband and aimed to please him at every turn. She also found joy in scamming and swindling gullible adventurers.

Possessions
Her most prized possession was a magical cloak of elvenkind, a wedding gift from Marilyn's mother.

History
Marilyn met Mortimer when she unsuccessfully tried to pickpocket the illusionist. To Marilyn's surprise, Mortimer asked the woman out instead of reporting her to the city guards. Their romanced mood at a break-neck speed. Soon after, the two tied the knot. She believed that Mortimer picked a wrong vocation and strove to teach him her thieving ways eventually.

During a spring or summer of the mid-14 century DR, Marilyn joined her husband and Elmerth Willowit, a fellow thief, on a scam aimed at traveling adventurers. Mortimer trained seven canaries with his magical ring and staged a scorched patch of grass to convince travelers he was a platinum dragon. Then he would approach travelers and ask them to support some faraway country's strife and ask for donations of gold and gems to pay for the goodly nation's defenses against evil. As the adventurers were distracted, Marilyn and Elmerth snuck to the victims and pickpocketed any remaining valuables from them. If Marilyn failed to lift the loot, she signaled her husband with a mirror, slipping away with the use of her cloak of elvenkind or a potion of flying.

During a spring or summer of the mid-14 century DR, a group of adventurers from Ravens Bluff, the Living City, came across the charlatan while traveling the forest. The result and successes of the interaction remained unrecorded. However, Mortimer was ready to use magic to scare adventurers into donating or fleeing using dust of disappearance. During that time, Mortimer Mittlemer and his wife used swindled treasure to invest in a certain lending institution and a popular tavern in Ravens Bluff.
