## Mask (object)

Masks were decorative clothing in the Realms used to cover one's face.

Description
Masks came with a variety of options, but the most common version covered the wearer's eyes.

Availability

 Aurora's Whole Realms Catalogue sold a variety of traditional comedy and tragedy theater masks, all finely painted and crafted from spruce, under its "Bards' Emporium" section at a cost of 5 gold pieces each. It also sold black pantomime masks for a singular gold piece and for 8 gold pieces offered masks representing animals or monsters, everyday archetypes, or concepts. These respectively included such things as bears, cats, dogs, ghosts, hawks, mice, orcs, and snakes; a king or queen, a merchant, a noble, a peasant, a slave, or a trickster; death, disease, fate, melancholy, and rage.
 Aurora's Whole Realms Catalogue also sold simple, black thieving masks, under its "Thieves' Corner" section. With a six month notice, customers could alternatively special order a mask that was designed to utterly disguise its wearer when in dim light.
 In Port Nyanzaru, masks among various other objects could be found for sale in the Grand Souk.

Varieties
Death mask otherwise known as a funerary mask, were a type of mask made to be laid upon the face of a deceased individual before burial rites. Many were made from fine metals, with gold bearded visages made for nobles typically valuing at around 44 gold pieces.
Domino mask A form of simple black mask that was commonly used by rogues.

Significance
Masks were sometimes worn on special occasions in the Realms, such as holidays. On Lliira's Night, it was common to see people wear star-shaped masks, while on Liar's Night people were encouraged to don all manner of masks. Though the most commonly worn masks on that holiday were those designed to depict the symbol of the god known as Mask and the mirror masks of the Leiran clergy.

Beyond their literal use, a number of organizations in the Realms featured masks as part of their symbol, such as the Night Masks, the Shadow Thieves, and the Church of Vhaeraun.

Notable Masks
 Andrathath's Mask
 Bone mask
 The Dragon masks, a series of five masks that were associated with the goddess Tiamat.
 The Faces of Madness, a group of seven a magical masks that were created by an alliance of Imaskari archmages known as the Cabal of Madness.
 Fanged mask
 Mask of beastliness, a magical mask that allowed a wearer to temporarily transform their head into that of a beast.
 Mask of the beast, a magical mask that enabled better communication with beasts.
 Mask of the Dragon Queen
 Mask of the five senses
 Mask of persuasion
 Mask of relentless compassion
 Moonstone mask
 Whispering mask, a variety of enchanted wooden masks that were used by the green hag Ethel to enthrall people.
 Winter's Mask

Notable Users
 Masks were worn by thieves or rogues to disguise their true identity.
Businesses
 The Moonstone Mask, a renowned festhall in Neverwinter, was so named for having all members of its staff wear glowing masks that were trimmed with moonstones.
Individuals
 Azaka Stormfang, wielder of the mask of the beast.
 Jalynfein, a powerful drow wizard who hid his disfigured face behind a featureless mask of grey cloth.

Organizations
 The members of the Night Masks typically wore domino masks.
 The Rogues of Tilverton all wore black silk face-masks that they kept stored in hidden compartments in Grimwald's Revenge.

Races & Sentient Creatures
 All batiri typically wore an oversized wooden war mask. Each mask was decorated and painted by its owner, designing them to intimidate their enemies. Besides being an article of clothing, these masks served the same purpose as coats of arms.
Religions
 The main altar in a Maskarran temple often had mask of silk floating above it.
 The priestly raiments of the Church of Leira included silvery, mirror-like masks.

## Mad Hermit

The man known only as the Mad Hermit was a Malarite serial killer who laired in the Neverwinter Wood in the late 14 century DR.

Description
The Mad Hermit was an old human man dressed in simple tattered robes permanently stained with browned blood stains. Underneath his robes, the man wore enchanted +2 scale mail and wielded a magic +3 greataxe.

History

Circa the, the Mad Hermit made a home in a Neverwinter Wood cave. The cave's opening had an unnerving air of menace about it, and an overhanging rock above was reminiscent of a dire beast's open maw. Inside, the Mad Hermit built a shrine and a sacrificial altar dedicated to his deity, Malar, the Black-Blooded One. Alongside the Hermit, the cave was home to two massive dire bears who served the Malarite. The shrine included a unique carved totem made of some unknown type of wood. It was light as if made of paper and smooth as if shaped by strange magics. The Mad Hermit fed many travelers to his beasts and captured other victims, only for them to be bled on the cave's altar. His victims were found with two small punctures on their necks next to each other.

## Makeup

Makeup was a term used for a wide variety of materials and substances, including powders and oils, that were applied to faces, usually for the purpose of coloring and beautifying them. Those who were skilled in applying makeup to the face of others were referred to as "makeup artists".

Description
Makeup was widely varied in form and application. Some substances, such as coal dust and tar, were used to blacken facial features, add dramatic lines, or to better conceal themselves in darkness. Conversely, some substances were used for the purposes of lightening features, such as flour. Some were used to add color, such as the cochineal powder of Maztica, which used to redden lips and cheeks. In the Anauroch, Bedine women used tanbark and turmeric for similar purposes. Makeup could also include skin putty, which was used to add circles beneath ones eyes or make their nose appear longer, and oil to add a sheen of gloss to one's skin.

Varieties
Cochineal A powder used on the lips and cheeks in Maztica, made from an endemic species of insects of the same name.
Kohl a thick black powder that was used by women in the land of Zakhara.
Lampblack a substance that was used by some thieves for the purposes of better concealing themselves within darkness.
Mrathaera lip glosses that were designed to dye, flavor, or scent the lips.
Tar makeup a makeup crafted from the substance of the same name that was similarly used for concealment purposes.

Availability
 In the city of Athkatla, makeup "touchover lasses" were often found congregating around the Flamewater Fountain.
 Aurora's Whole Realms Catalogue sold general makeup kits under its "Bards' Emporium" section for 25 gold pieces, as well as a jar of tar makeup under its "Thieves' Corner" section for 3 gp.
 The Bards Guild of Ravens Bluff was host to a great deal of thespians that were considered to be the best makeup artists in the city and earned a lot of coin from doing the makeup of the vainer lords and ladies of the city prior to public ceremonies or important revels.
 Facemaker's Boutique, a clothing store in Baldur's Gate that helped its customers with makeup and other cosmetic services.
 Yathla Oloryn, an expert makeup maker that lived in the city-state of Calaunt around 1358 DR.

Usages
 In some mortuaries, such as that of the Daggerford Graveyard, light applications of makeup and blush were used on corpses to make them more presentable during funerals.
 Beyond making them more presentable, some utilized makeup on corpses to try and disguise them as other people.
Magic
 Friends required a spellcaster to apply makeup to their own face. Older versions of the spell specifically required the use of lampblack.

Notable Users
 Makeup was widely favored by performers, such as bards and jesters, to either enhance or disguise their facial features.
Individuals
 Pristoleph, a fire genasi that applied makeup in an effort to pass himself off as a human of Chondathan ethnicity.
Races & Sentient Creatures
 The Reigar, a race of androgynous spacefaring humanoids, widely used makeup and attached no gender distinctions towards it.
 Vampires sometimes wore blush and makeup in order to conceal their undead nature.

Regions, Nations, & Settlements
 In the nation of Thay, those of poorer standing sometimes used makeup to draw temporary designs on their shaved heads in lieu of the the tattoos that were widespread in the nation.
 In the Netherese Empire, it was quite common for people to heavily apply makeup.

The book collected recipes that utilized foodomancy to create various enchanted foods. The recipes included diagrams, precise directions, and exact measurements, as well as the ingredients required for each dish. ## Maladweomer

Maladweomer was a spell utilized by wizards to manipulate the effectiveness of spells and magical powers cast by targeted creatures.

Effects
When cast, the spell imposed a state of diminished effectiveness on all spells and spell-like powers used by the targeted creature. Offensive magical attacks inflicted only minimal damage. Additionally, any ongoing spells or enchantments active on the target at the time of spell's effect were modified in efficacy.

The reverse of this spell, dweomerboost, was also known as empradweomer. Dweomerboost empowered the recipient creature to cast or wield magic at its maximum efficiency.

Components
In addition to verbal and somatic components, this spell required a material component, a small clear glass or crystal prism that was forcefully shattered during the spellcasting process. However, when dweomerboost was cast, the crystal or glass simply vanished upon the completion of the spellcasting

## Magic missile, dukar seeker

Magic missile, dukar seeker was a unique adaptation of the traditional magic missile spell.

Effects
When cast, this spell generated up to five ethereal missiles that sprung forth from the caster's fingertip, precisely homing in on their intended target. Each missile inflicted damage similar to the standard magic missile spell. However, what sets this variant apart is its distinct focus on targeting Dukars.

If there were Dukars within the spell's range, the magical missiles prioritized seeking them out over any other potential targets. In the event that the caster designated a non-Dukar as the target while one or more Dukars were within range, the missiles automatically redirected themselves towards the closest available Dukar within range. Conversely, if the caster specifically selected one or more Dukars as targets within range, the missiles unerringly flew towards the designated Dukar(s), regardless of proximity to other potential Dukar targets.

Upon impact, these specialized missiles delivered additional damage when striking a Dukar. The extra damage inflicted increased incrementally with each subsequent missile hitting the target.

Components
This spell only required a verbal component.

## Marckarius Millithor

Marckarius Millithor was the elderboy of House Millithor in the 14 century DR.

Description
Marckarius had a somewhat unusual look for a drow, as his hair was very short; he found this gave him an advantage in combat. The muscular elderboy was not as tall or lithe as a typical drow, though his arms were much longer than usual.

His clothing was of a very high quality, and was woven with thread of silver and even platinum.

Personality
The elderboy of House Millithor liked to be different to others from Menzoberranzan, and indeed, he was. Though he was both chaotic and wicked, he was a lot more sociable then others and enjoyed light-hearted pleasures. He was particularly careful of how he dressed.

The son of Ki'Willis Millithor was exceptionally loyal, particularly to his mother, whom found him to be of very high value. In return, she granted him privileges and freedom far beyond the norm for a drow male. Even though he was wary of dealing with other houses and priestesses, his freedom allowed him to be assertive, even to the priestesses of his own house.

Marckarius's desire was to grow old and be granted ultimate freedom, and for his house to survive and flourish.

Abilities
This heavily-armored and strong drow warrior was a skilled combatant, and was able to throw daggers up to .

Possessions
Marckarius wore an expensive cloak, a shirt, leggings, a piwafwi, boots of elvenkind, and an amulet of proof against detection and location, which he kept hidden. To armor himself, he wore chainmail +3 and a buckler +1.

His primary weapon was a longsword +4, and his secondary weapons were considered to be a shortsword +2 and a pair of sleeved daggers +2.

In addition to weapons and armor, Marckarius was careful to bring with him potions kept in metal flasks, themselves kept in a back pouch. These potions were of extra-healing, invisibility, and flying.

The drow also possessed a great worth of gold and jewelery totalling nearly 10,000 gp. His rare jewelery consisted of emerald and ruby rings, earrings made of different types of gems, and a diamond necklace. He only wore these on social occasions, and never in battle.

## Masks of the Dohi-ri

Heroes of the Living Jungle participated in the annual Dohi-ri celebration – the Festival of the Mask, Zurich which they embarked on a journey to assemble and decorate masks from the boon of the jungle. They confronted a tribe of slaver tasloi, a band of leopard katanga pretending to be fellow Festival Walkers, visited an ancient shrine to an ancestor grippli race, parleyed with an evil nereid and a peaceful water naga. Eventually, one of the heroes was named the new Masked One, and their mask was enchanted.

## Magician's Row

Magician's Row was a street in Ravens Bluff named for the number of wizards who dwelled there in the mid–14 century DR.

Description
It was a short stretch of only five houses, each of different colors, styles, sizes, and states of disrepair. They were:
 Yellow, one story: home of Norweg the Magnificent
 Blue, two story: home of Ukran the Great
 Red, two story: home of Glishman the Annoying
 Gray, single story: home of Paniar the Obese
 Green, two stories: home of Panese the Excitable

History
Circa 1357 DR, Norweg and Panese separately stole two minor magic items of historical importance from the city vaults at approximately the same time. Though the thieves were unidentified, clues at the crime scenes, suspicions, and divinations tracked them to Magician's Row. The City Guard serving Regent of the Exchequer Vernon Condor only had time to search two of the five houses before they earned their boss's ire, so they tried to deduce the culprits from what they knew of the five wizards on Magician's Row.

## Masters of This Hall

Masters of This Hall was a popular book of drama and wordplay in the Heartlands of the Realms.

Contents

The book told the tale of an aged king who died with six warlike and rival sons vying for the throne. Arriving to stake their claim, the princes are forestalled by the high priests of the realm gathered in the throne room, and having used their divine magic to prevent swords and arrows from being used. The ambitious princes are thus given an ultimatum: they must each use their rhetoric to persuade the collected priests that they are the most worthy of being king, and must swear fealty to the chosen king before leaving, else be slain by the priest's spells. As such, the book was largely made up of well-written back-and-forths between the various princes and priests as they debate, boast, argue, interrogate, and generally word-fence at each other.

History

The book was already very old and considered a classic by the 14 century DR, and underwent a great many reprintings and new editions, sometimes with amendments by those who thought they could improve on the original. It was considered a good source for witticisms, and was frequently quoted by its readers.

## Matthew Hopkins

Matthew Hopkins was an eccentric, but well-respected, necromancer member of the Ministry of Art in the late 14 century DR.

Description
In the 1370s DR, Matthew was an older man whose mental capacities were diminished with age and made him prone to fits of frustrated rage. He was a white-haired man in his 70s.

Abilities
Matthew kept two active protective spells cast on himself most of the time: armor and stoneskin. Because of his lunacy, any attempts to use the ESP magic on him rendered the casters prone to be paralyzed and curled up in the fetal position, overwhelmed by his mind.

History
He was born sometime in the early 1300s or late 1290s DR. In spring of the, Matthew Hopkins posted a wanted ad in the Ravens Bluff Trumpeter broadsheet. He requested a single vial of a female tanar'ri's dying breath, bottled for under six hours. Matthew claimed that the vial for required for his research and offered to pay 5,000 gold pieces for it.

A band of heroes of the Living City answered Matthew's classified and were escorted to his elegantly decorated study in the Ministry of Art. Along with the aged mage, Camille Hopkins greeted the adventurers. However, the woman they met was not human, but a glassteel construct of a beautiful young woman. Camille once was Matthew's late wife. The mage acted and conversed with the mindless construct as if it were his dear wife, yet the real Camille was trapped on the Prime Material plane as a ghost. In his utter madness, Matthew concocted a ritual to imbue the construct with his wife's spring, "bringing her back to life," and he needs a dying breath of a succubus or an alu-fiend. Matthew claimed that she was tortured to death by Loviatans, but in his madness, he suppressed memory of himself being a Pain of Loviatar and was the person who performed the ritual on behest of the goddess that killed Camille.

The accords of the adventurers' actions varied. By one statement, they fulfilled the delivery for the mad wizard and let him perform the non-existent ritual with the bottled dying breath that turned the construct hostile, sending it into a destructive rage. Another version of the events talked about them confronting the wizard and calling out his madness, which infuriated Camille's ghost and resulted in a scuffle. Whatever the outcome might had been, the Ministry of Art was not happy with the adventurers and the battle that spilled out of the wizard's study. The adventurers were blamed, as Matthew Hopkins committed no crime, legally-speaking.

## Mallus

Mallus was a tall human fighter in the late 14 century DR who died while on an expedition in the Shining Sea after becoming infected by olive slimes.

History
In the, sometime around the month of Flamerule, a group of eccentric entertainers, entrepreneurs, and scientists embarked upon a colonizing expedition to an island they discovered in the Shining Sea off the coast of Chult, which they dubbed the "Forgotten Island". Led by a charismatic Waukeenar priest named Devlin, they sought to create a tourist attraction on the isle that would attract people from all across the Realms. Three months later, things began to go awry for the expedition.

On Marpenoth 11, five velociraptors infected with olive slimes attacked the campsite's messhall. The group managed to slay them all, but not without Mallus becoming injured and his fellow fighter Argus dying. Unbeknownst to the group, Mallus had become infected by the velociraptors with olive slime and would gradually infect all but Devlin. Sailing off the island began to be considered, but could not be pursued as heavy storms kept everyone in the campsite over Marpenoth 13 and 14. On the 14, well before dawn, Devlin observed Mallus devouring a day's worth of rations in the camp's kitchen. He later expressed in his diary that he felt Mallus had gone insane, but attributed it to possibly being a fever. When the storms finally let up on Marpenoth 16, the group went to the docks and discovered their ships were wrecked, thus stranding them on the island. All members of the crew were dejected by this turn of events, though Mallus was strangely calm over the matter.

The next day, it was noted by Devlin that Mallus had stopped sleeping and had spread his condition to Ledro Kile, and he had observed them together eating a dinosaur raw in the center of camp. Surmising that Mallus had likely spread his malady to everyone that shared the barracks, Devlin barred his villa door. The next morning, Marpenoth 18, Devlin looked out his window to find that Mallus had fully metamorphosed into a slime creature—his once handsome features replaced with a spongy, green substance. Recognizing that Mallus had lost his humanity, Devlin surmised it would only be a matter of time before he was infected as well. The rest of the camp recognized that Mallus had physically changed in some manner, but were too deluded by their own infections to be put off by it. Mallus went on to tell them all that Devlin had gone insane, before proceeding to burn most of the group's magic items at the camp's trashpit.

On the night of Marpenoth 19, Devlin snuck into the barracks and engaged the transformed Mallus in battle, who at that point only had parts of his skeleton remaining.  After killing Mallus, Devlin proceed to murder everyone else in the barracks while they were in their beds. Examining their bodies, Devlin found bits of olive slime on all, confirming his suspicions. Devlin worked to scrape the ooze off all but Mallus, then burned the scrapings in a wicker basket before proceeding to burn the bodies of everyone inside the barracks. Before hanging himself the next day, Mallus's name and the names of the rest of the expedition crew would be recorded by Devlin in the last entry of his diary.

## Malus Thorm

Malus Thorm was a surgeon and servant of the goddess Shar, who operated out of the House of Healing in the town of Reithwin throughout the 15 century DR.

Description
The once-noble elf's body had become twisted both by the darkness of the shadow-cursed lands and what appeared to be self-performed surgeries and mechanical "enhancements". His undead flesh was gray and pocked with boils and bruises. He had replaced both of his arms with mechanical claws that had scalpels for fingers. Undead flesh and metal extensions had been grafted to his legs, making him unnaturally tall.

He wore a black tailcoat trimmed with gold, complete with padded upper sleeves and a ruffled collar. Over his brow he wore a leather harness that supported goggles with dark lenses, and magnifier that resembled Shar's holy symbol.

Personality

Malus believed his surgical work, really his twisted experimentation, was the true expression of Shar's will.

Abilities
If forced to engage a foe in combat, Malus would utilize his four instruments of loss: a bonesaw, a syringe, a trepan, or the application of leeches.

Possessions
Malus wore around his neck a surgeon's subjugation amulet, a necklace that could be used to paralyze his patients when necessary.

He owned a copy of the book Surgery and Physiology: A Sharran's Primer, a medical dissertation written from the perspective of Sharran physicians. He also kept within his office a pair of poisoner's gloves.

Relationships

Malus Thorm was General Ketheric Thorm's uncle.

Malus was served by four undead pupils, Sisters Anya, Geanne, Hunna, and Vanessa, among others. He was not wholly confident in their abilities, and believed the incisions they made were not exactly precise. In truth they were little more than outright butchers.

In the late 14 century DR Sister Anna Lidwin wrote an urgent letter to Baldur's Gate seeking aid as she could not dare argue with Malus Thorm who ordered to heal only the Dark Justiciars and conducted experiments on the others.

There was a constant dispute between Malus and Ketheric's advisor Balthazar, as the both needed corpses for their own purposes. The necromancer Balthazar confiscated the most valuable cadavers providing Malus with separate body parts in best case as follows from the Surgeon's Tissue and Organ Register found in the House of Healing's Morgue.

Activities

As of the late 15 century DR, Malus and his nurses operated out of the House of Healing in the Shadow-cursed lands. He spent much of his time "experimenting" on innocents that either wandered, or were brought against their will, into his hospital. Malus attempted to teach his students the finer arts of what he referred to as surgery, but was ultimately unsuccessful.

## Marlel

Marlel, known as the The Dark Blade of Doom, was an infamous assassin of Scornubel in the mid–14 century DR. He was a retainer for the Cult of the Dragon, but also a Harper.

Personality
Marlel was pleased by the slaying of malevolent mages and potential rivals. He seized short-term pleasures wherever the opportunity rose and he liked good food. Also, he was cautious and hard to catch unaware.

Abilities
Not merely an ace with the blade, Marlel had a number of skills, including disguise and sewing, though his expertise regarding blandreths was limited. A number of wenches attested he did everything well. The Dark Blade of Doom was also capable of wielding wands.

Relationships
Marlel was on retainer for the Cult of the Dragon, through Thoadrin. Belgon Bradaskor was dismissive of his assumed name. He claimed to have business with Orthil Voldovan.

Possessions
Marlel hid daggers on his person. He wore a ring that carried spells, and always hid a few needles and waxed thread on a shoe. He was furnished with a number of "masks", which could be damaged in combat, and which cost at least five quara. He also carried on himself an armorweave bag. The assassin was paid a hefty retainer by the Dragon Cult and bore a Harper pin.

Appearance
Marlel's sly expression somewhat resembled Torm's. He was black-haired, when out of costume.

Reputation
His reputation as the Dark Blade of Doom had reached the Red Wizards of Thay, and some Zhentarim spies were able to pick him out on sight, despite his disguises.

History
Marlel claimed to have worked with a Red Wizard in Triel prior to 1357 DR. By the end of that year, he had been in Scornubel for about five seasons, through which he'd become a retainer for the Cult of the Dragon. He had at some point delivered "doom" upon a number of Sembians, presumably during those five seasons.

Late in the, Marlel met with Thoadrin, a Dragon Cult operative in Scornubel. Along the way, he was attacked by three people, and slew all of them. Marlel was able to correctly ascertain he was going to be ordered to hunt for spellfire; his payment consisted of fifty Calimshan rubies, with fifty more to be paid upon completion.

He caught up with the spellfire wielder Shandril Shessair in the Scornubian inn known as the Sun over Scornubel, assisting her when a number of Zhentarim swordsmen tried to capture her. After aiding her in her escape, he led her towards the Stormy Tankard, where he brought her and her husband, Narm Tamaraith, to the local Harpers, and then to an ambush with numerous wizards. They employed spells against Shandril and Narm, knocking him out, but then Shandril slew them all. Marlel was able to convince her he had no part in the ambush; however the laying of Marlel's ambush was known to Tornar, who later reported to Belgon Bradaskor that it had failed. The Dark Blade of Doom showed her to her room, and then pointed out Orthil Voldovan, whom she was seeking, in the common room of the inn.

Marlel entered Orthil Voldovan's caravan disguised as a religious pilgrim paying for covered passage to Waterdeep, concerned with his own piety and unable to use holy magic, who had nonetheless declined to name the god that was the reason for his pilgrimage. While in the caravan, he lured Haransau Olimer and his assistant to another wagon, which he destroyed with a couple spells, killing Haransau in the process; he then impersonated Haransau Olimer. During one ambush, Marlel's disguise was sliced along the belly; he managed to slay two brigands and then hid to reconstruct his disguise. He was able to stitch his fake belly back together quickly, successfully fooling Arauntar and Beldimarr with his disguise.

During his time impersonating the blandreth-dealer, Marlel spread some rumors to make obstacles for the other rogues in the caravan, bringing up the clinking of the wagon on which Mhegras and Sabran traveled to ensure they were searched. While spying, he bore witness to Narm slaying a man who attempted to ambush him in the night; Marlel considered the dying man to be a Thayan agent. Later, Marlel slew a Zhentarim disguised as a merchant during one ambush. During another ambush, Stlarakur, a Zhentarim priest of Bane, thought to take refuge in Haransau Olimer's wagon. Marlel took the opportunity to brain the man with a blandreth, and left his body at the wagon's entrance, with one arm outside to deter anyone else from taking refuge there.

While the caravan remained at Triel, the Dark Blade of Doom was contacted by a voice out of thin air; he chose to heed it, and it gave him a mission. Once the caravan arrived at Triel, Marlel took a moment to meet with Hulrivior and his underlings; he introduced himself as having worked with a Red Wizard sometime prior in Triel, and offered them spellfire. While their guard was down, he threw a gem into a flame hovering on the table atop the meeting room, leading to a terrible explosion, which almost certainly killed Hulrivior, per Marlel's understanding. He then used wands to execute any survivors, claiming it was another Red Wizard that hired him to slay them. Hesperdan claimed responsibility for Marlel being in possession of such magic.

Marlel attempted to wield an unspecified wand of some flame power against Shandril while she was undergoing meltdown. One of his spell blows was blocked by Mirt, who threw himself in the way; this won Shandril enough time that she was ready for his next attack, and returned spellfire along its way, killing Marlel instantly.

## Magical Histories

Magical Histories was a multi-volume book that collected history and lore on the topic of magic, published before 1492 DR.

Content
Volume I: The Origins of Mystra
The tome focused on the first incarnation of the Goddess of Magic, Mystryl, who was said to had been born from a primordial battle between light and darkness, the deities Selûne and Shar. Each of the divine sisters shed a portion of their magic into a new deity – a being of pure Art. As such, Mystryl became the absolute mistress of all magic in the world, forming it into the weave, a way to harness magic. She was the weave.

The book continued to describe the, when Mystryl perished and was reborn as the new goddess of magic – Mystra, as the outcome of the Karsus's Folly, the ancient event in which Netherese lord Karsus sought to take the magic of Mystryl for himself. She ended her own existence to stop Karsus from achieving his goals, temporarily unweaving all magic in the world, which became the end of the Netherese Empire.

History
In the, a copy of Magical Histories Volume 1: The Origins of Mystra was kept in the Stormshore Tabernacle multi-deity temple located in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate, near its shrine to the Mother of All Magic, Mystra.

## Mardon's Mountaineering

Mardon's Mountaineering was a school in Eileanar that taught practical mountaineering skills.

Services
The school was attended by those that sought to scale the many forbidding and peaks and glaciers of Netheril without relying on magic, such as the magic-blocking Widowmaker Mountain. They were taught the necessary skills via a set of artificial climbing walls that got progressively more complicated and difficult as they introduced more obstacles and unclimbable surfaces. The building was left open-roofed so that climbers were exposed to inclement weather, and the instructors often performed their tests during active storms so as to truly test their students. Thanks to the use of quasimagical items such as rings of feather fall, there were no fatalities within the school. It usually took about three months of intensive training to fully prepare a student for real-world climbing, costing the trainee about 150 gp plus any equipment needed.

## Many-Arrows tribe

The Many-Arrows tribe, also written as the Many Arrows tribe, was the most powerful mountain orc tribe in the North and one of the most successful and notorious orc tribes in all of Faerûn during the 14 and 15 centuries DR. It was not a single tribe, but an amalgam of tribes subsumed by force into the tribe of Obould Many-Arrows or which dwelt within the Kingdom of Many-Arrows.

Organization
The Many-Arrows tribe comprised several tribes of orcs, and following the creation of the Kingdom of Many-Arrows, half-orcs as well. One such orc tribe was the Broken Arrow tribe, to which the Obould dynasty belonged.

The Many-Arrows' symbol was a crudely rendered humanoid skull that was pierced by three arrows.

Activities

Torture
Prior to the founding of the Kingdom of Many-Arrows, the Many Arrows orcs were renowned for their cruelty. Non-orc prisoners were branded as slaves and either put to work in mines—where they quickly died of injury or starvation—or were shackled and forced to serve an orc master, who was liable to torture or kill them on a whim. The exception to this was elves, who were typically killed brutally. Children, halflings, and gnomes, were tormented as a form of entertainment, while and anyone the orcs regarded as exotic was caged and pressed for information about treasure. Torture was generally seen as a fun pastime, and extracting information from a torture victim was an afterthought. If a victim claimed to know of a secret cache of treasure, they might be freed from immediate captivity to be allowed to guide the orcs to the location, with human mercenaries sometimes being employed to follow the person into cities or other places where orcs dared not go. Inevitably, the orcs' plan was to claim the treasure and then kill whoever had led them to it.

Feasts and Festivals
Celebrations of orcish holidays and gods were marked by great feasts at which all could gorge themselves on food and drink as well as enjoy the killing of elves. Such festivities were used by King Obould to placate his followers and prevent uprisings, but required a large amount of money, which in turn led him both to open trade with humans and to order his guards to steal from his own orc raiders.

Trade
The Many-Arrows tribe was long known for manufacturing orcish weapons and armor, which they traded with other orc tribes and beyond. While they occupied the Citadel of Many Arrows prior to the mid-to-late 14 century DR, they also were known to trade in illicit or stolen goods as well as slaves. Their own slave labor force was predominantly humans and goblins.

Tactics
The tribe used scouts and skirmishers to observe and test enemy defenses and to map the terrain of future battles in order to secure strategic advantages. When preparing for war against the cities of the North, they constructed great siege engine.

Base of Operations
Prior to the mid-to-late 14 century DR, the tribe was based in the Citadel of Many Arrows. After being driven from this fortress-city, they retreated to Dark Arrow Keep, which would go on to become the capital of their Kingdom of Many Arrows through the late 15 century DR.

Possessions
They favored black scimitars and their fiercest warriors wore distinctive belts decorated with the traditional totems of the tribe. Some were known to carry—and sometimes to give as gifts—orc stones, which could summon the spirits of orcish warriors in combat.

Relationships
The tribe had many enemies. Prior to their ouster from the Citadel of Many Arrows, their foes included all of the human and dwarven realms of the North, and any non-orc who arrived in the Citadel without Obould's protection would end up dead: only a select few human and half-orc merchants and mercenaries tended to be allowed inside. They maintained spies in most human communities of the North, although they notably struggled to infiltrate Everlund, Neverwinter, and Silverymoon. They were also opposed to the forces of Hellgate Keep, and came to regard other orcs with suspicion as their shamans predicted that the Citadel would fall to orcish treachery.

After they were driven from the Citadel, they became the most feared orcs in the North within just a few years. The folk of the Silver Marches were constantly on-guard for what they knew was an inevitable attack from Many-Arrows. They were also no friends to the tanarukks of the North. During this time, the tribe grew by consolidating other tribes, and so internal restlessness and treachery remained a large concern, causing the orcs to spy on each other.

After the signing of the Treaty of Garumn's Gorge in the mid-to-late 14 century DR, they entered into a tenuous peace with the realms of the North. While they remained enemies, they traded and even worked together on occasion, which was sufficient to earn the Kingdom of Many-Arrows a reputation as a realm of orcs who valued civilization. As of the 1470s DR, tensions had risen with neighboring Luruar and Mithral Hall, they were warring with the Uthgardt barbarians, and they had come into conflict with Neverwinter following an incursion by their raiders into the ruins of the north of that city. Their only notable ally at that time was Netheril.

History
Citadel of Many Arrows
The Many-Arrows tribe had its roots in Dead Orc Pass in the Rauvin Mountains. The tribe took its name from the Citadel of Many Arrows, which was in turn named for the Battle of Many Arrows in which the orcs overran and claimed the Citadel from Silverymoon in the . They ruled the Citadel for centuries, during which time they fended off numerous attacks from Silverymoon and Sundabar. By the mid-to-late 14 century DR, and their numbers had swelled to 40,000, leaving them living in cramped and impoverished conditions. The threat of starvation drove many of them to beg, steal, or take up arms to raid caravans and capture slaves. Their raiders harried traffic on the roads between Silverymoon and Sundabar, and occasionally tested the defenses of the cities themselves. The ill-gotten goods from these raids were sold to evil human merchants (with many of these products finding their ways to Everlund). They also traded in orcish weapons and armor, which were produced in the Citadel using metal seized in raids or dug up by slaves.

While it was long thought that the orcs were too numerous to dislodge from their Citadel, this changed in the . In late summer of that year, an orc horde of 150,000 led by King Greneire arrived at the Citadel, and King Obould and his shamans—believing that Greneire had come to usurp the Citadel—declared the horde to be full of traitors who were to be slaughtered "like elves during a festival." This incited a siege that lasted for four months, during which the Many-Arrows orcs began to die off from increasingly poor living conditions despite inflicting greater losses on their foes. Finally, in the first tenday of Uktar, King Greneire threw his full might against the Citadel and broke through the gates, and the Citadel was set alight. In the ensuring battle, Obould and Greneire faced each other in a legendary duel that ended with Obould badly injured and Greneire dead. During this climactic battle, a force of dwarves and humans led by Emerus Warcrown arrived and routed the exhausted orcs, driving them from the Citadel.

Dark Arrow Keep
Reduced to only about 4,500 survivors, the orcs fled to the Spine of the World, and for a short time, it was unknown whether King Obould had survived his injuries. In fact he had, and he led a few hundred of his best warriors to capture Dark Arrow Keep—an old orcish castle that had been claimed by giants—and established this fortress as his new base. About half of the tribe moved into the fortress, while the rest settled in caves in the nearby mountains.

With his new citadel secured, Obould plotted to reclaim his old home from the dwarves. To this end, he began probing for weak points in the Silver Marches alliance while absorbing rival tribes and gathering the orcs of the mountains into a massive horde. Exactly how he managed to bend so many wild orc tribes to his will was a mystery, but he managed the seemingly impossible feat of inspiring loyalty in them akin to that seen in the monarchies of the south (even a century later, scholars remained unsure of how he had accomplished this). Soon, rumors of Obould's new horde had made him into a boogeyman for the people of the Silver Marches and elevated his tribe to new levels of infamy. Guided by the advice of the drow Ad'non Kareese, he navigated a tense alliance with Gerti Orelsdottr, leader of the frost giants of Shining White, and their joint forces began conducting raids against travelers around the Spine of the World. Soon, Obould's aspirations turned to the establishment of an orc empire large enough to be divided among his eight sons.

Kingdom of Many-Arrows

As the people of a kingdom, the Many-Arrows orcs managed to coexist relatively peacefully with the humans of the North, although they continued to fight amongst each other and it was clear that peace was only tenuous at best. A century after the realm's founding, they had faced civil wars and ongoing conflicts with the Uthgardt barbarians, and it was primarily the kings (all descendants of Obould, and who assumed his name once they became king) who were interested in peace. Nevertheless, the orcs of Many-Arrows gained renowned as the rare example of "civilized" orcs.

In the late 1470s DR, King Obould XVII sent a contingent of orcs led by Vansi Bloodscar to scout the ruins of Neverwinter, which had been destroyed by a cataclysm decades prior. However, Bloodscar defied her orders and instead led her troops to occupy parts of the northern half of the city. By the, these orcs—including Bloodscar herself—had fallen under the sway of the Abolethic Sovereignty, and were effectively in open rebellion against Many-Arrows as they pursued their own interests.

The experiment with peace ended in the, when the orcs marched on Luruar in the War of the Silver Marches. This conflict came about when the rightful heir to the throne, Lorgru, was usurped by a warmonger called Hartusk. The war ended in the summer of the, when Bruenor Battlehammer led an alliance of dwarves against Dark Arrow Keep, killing Chief Hartusk and capturing the city. Meanwhile, Lorgru was restored as the leader of Many-Arrows, and the kingdom's surviving forces rallied behind him. Although Lorgru desired to continue the legacy of living in relative peace with the realms to the south, Bruenor had lost faith in the ability for the orcs to coexist with the Silver Marches. He thus banished Lorgru and his followers into the mountains and completely leveled Dark Arrow Keep, thus ending the Kingdom of Many-Arrows.

Nevertheless, the Many-Arrows tribe was still by far the most powerful orc tribe in the Spine of the World, and remained famous for their legacies of both peace and war. As of the, a Many-Arrows hunting party might still be willing to parlay rather than fight, especially if greeted in the Orc language or offered a gift that could not be easily taken by force. Such hunting parties were known to range as far as Icewind Dale.

Members
Some tribes comprising the Many-Arrows tribe included:
 The Bloodblade tribe
 The Broken Arrow tribe
 The Dust-Treader tribe
 The Green Moss tribe

## Mapper's Workshop

The Mapper's Workshop was a small shop in the city of Ravens Bluff, operated by the mage Jork Marpe in the 14 century DR, that sold maps and various other kinds of paper products.

Location
This shop was originally tucked away within an alley, near the riverfront in the district of Crow's End. It later moved locations to the Harbor District's neighborhood Bitterstone, in a building that stood at the corner of Black Visor Street and the Rhabie Promenade.

Structure
At both of its locations the shop was housed within a ramshackled wooden building. A faded, scrawled sign hung above their doors that read "Pictures Drawn."

The original storefront consisted of an office room that customers were never allowed beyond, two storage rooms that were well organized, a library, and three bedrooms. The front door had a broken lock, which led the store to never have valuable merchandise out on display.

The office room in the original storefront was filled with all manner of tables for drafting and scribing. His desk was well-cared for and made of polished walnut, but typically found covered in papers and quills, with drawers jammed full of parchment scrolls and various mugs. The Workshop's tables all had magic on them that made papers adhered to them so they wouldn't move while the mage worked. They could only be removed by applying an exotic ink with an intricate stamp bearing Jork's mage sigil.

Reputation
This Mapper's Workshop was a rather obscure business in Ravens Bluff. It was largely unknown to the city's officials, as well as the Merchants Guild, being as it wasn't even registered with the guild. Most of its business was generated by word of mouth. The majority of its clientele were adventurers, though far-traveled merchants were also known to visit it.

Jork Morpe's distaste for young adventurers, his ever inquisitive insistence that customers inform him of their reasons for wanting to purchase any of his merchandise, and the ill-temper that was expressed whenever the hard-of-hearing mage was misunderstood, were found to be quite irritating to some. The cantankerous mage attempted to be cordial with customers, but often fell flat. Later on he began asking customers to write down their requests for him, understanding that shouting to get through to him could be tiresome, Despite these issues, the Mapper's Workshop managed to maintain regular customers who were accustomed to Jork's quick-temper and hearing issues. Having a keen memory, clients were always remembered by the mage.

Services
Being the namesake of the Mapper's Workshop, the shop sold a wide selection of geographical maps of places all across Faerûn, as well as comprehensive maps of the sewers of Ravens Bluff and fragments of those maps. The store also stocked a few maps of various countries that existed on the world of Oerth, particularly those that neighbored the city-state of Greyhawk, having been gifted them by a well-traveled merchant that spoke highly of Oerth. Most of the maps sold at the shop were supplied by Jork's two adventuring sons, though Jork did make a few of them himself and would spend painstaking hours to create copies of his most popular maps. Jork also occasionally hired adventurers to explore the under-detailed areas of his maps.

Besides maps, the Workshop sold diagrams of gnomish inventions, sketches of ruined keeps, detailed drawing of suits of armor, and schematics of the homes of Ravenian nobles (acquired from thieves).

Maps were priced according to each customer's age, appearance, and the urgency of their need for it. Those under the age of 50 were comparatively charged more than those who weren't. If clients lacked enough gold pieces for a purchase the proprietor was willing to negotiate a bargain for valuable items, jewelry, and weapons. And if a map couldn't be afforded, he was willing to offer a glimpse for a price, though he would not extend this offer for one-of-a-kind maps.

History
Sometime in the 14 century DR, the necromancer Artemus visited the Mapper's Workshop and inquired about purchasing the store's map of the city's sewers. Jork informed the necromancer that he would have to wait and come back a few days after he had made a copy of it. Unwilling to wait, Artemus broke into the Workshop later and stole it. A few days later a group of adventurers came into the shop seeking the same map, but Jork had only a partial copy to offer them at a cost of 80 gold pieces. He was willing to tell the adventurers all the details he could remember about Artemus, though only if they paid him a bribe of 30 or 60 gp.

## Mama Angleiron

The woman simply known as Mama Angleiron was the mother of the master smith, an aspiring writer, and the proprietor of Rivington General, Gyldro Angleiron in the mid-to-late 15 century DR.

History
Mama Angleiron was the mother of Master Gyldro and some unrevealed number of his siblings. Despite Having a close relationship with his Mama, Gyldro was a lonely and sensitive soul. By the, he developed a case of melancholy that worried Mama Angleiron. She tried to encourage the master blacksmith via petter to seek professional help. His depression likely was the result of loneliness and a broken heart. Despite her pleads, Gyldro seemed be resistant to the idea.

## Marten (creature)

Martens were a species of mustelid or "weasel", a family of small mammals that included ferrets and weasels.

Description
These animals were similar in appearance to other mustelids, being small and slender-bodied furry creatures. They measured around  in length and weighed around . Much like other mustelids, martens were skilled swimmers.

Ecology
Diet
These creatures were a carnivorous species.

Habitats
Like other mustelids, martens could be found in a wide variety of climates, though they more commonly inhabited cooler ones. They generally preferred to avoid dense settlements.

In north Faerûn, they could be found in parts of the Dalelands, particularly Daggerdale and Deepingdale. In northwest Faerûn they could be found in the Silver Marches.

Beyond Faerûn, martens could be found across much of the continent of Kara-Tur, living in temperate forests and plains as well as tropical and sub-tropical forests.

Relationships
Some wizards were known to have martens as familiars.

Usage
The hides of these creatures were quite valued, ranking among the most prized pelts of the Silver Marches. They were valued more than the hides of ferrets, stoats, and weasels, while they were typically valued less than those of ermines, minks, and sables, though they could fetch comparable prices.

The marten pelts of the Silver Marches were carried and traded all across the Sword Coast, while those of the Dalelands were traded by the Silverhand House coster to the cities of Arabel and Ordulin. In the trading posts of Everlund and Silverymoon, marten pelts could fetch anywhere from 2 to 8 gold pieces. In the further-off markets of Luskan, Neverwinter, and Waterdeep they were sold for twice those amounts. Aurora's Whole Realms Catalogue sold marten hides at a flat rate of 8 gold pieces each.

Trivia
In the church of Baervan Wildwanderer, "Marten" was one of the titles for confirmed priests, ranking directly above "Hedgehog" and below "Red Fox".

## Matilda the White Lady

Matilda the White Lady was one of the retired adventurers inhabiting Nellie Thursday Home for Experienced Adventurers sometime in the mid-to-late 14 century DR.

Description
Matilda was a  tall tough woman of . Her hair was silvered with age and eyes - blue. The White Lady had a blustering personality in contrast to her subdued and quiet husband.

Possessions
In her long life, the White Lady accumulated some impressive magic items: an enchanted +2 white chain mail, a magical +1 shield, and wielded a scimitar of speed. She carried potions of extra healing, potions of hill giant strength, and potions of speed, all of some dubious potency due to being created forty years prior.

The White Lady was an avid reader of the Good Castlekeeping monthly periodical.

Abilities
Matilda was fluent in several languages: Common, Elvish, and Orcish. As a fighter, she specialized in battling with scimitars and was trained to wield flails, lances, spears, short swords, and more exotic bastard swords. The White Lady had impressive endurance, could battle blinded, and was a capable horseback rider, swimmer, and a talented needle-point seamstress.

History
Matilda the White Lady and her husband of forty years, Henry the Shadow Master, retired to Nellie Thursday Home for Experienced Adventurers together. Nellie Thursday became Matilda's good friend for the entire thirty years the couple spent at the kindly dwarf's retirement community. After retirement, Matilda managed to achieve a great feat – convincing Henry to stop smoking. The two enjoyed the time at Nellie Thursday, its elegant lodgings, and even a training area where the eighty-nine-year-old adventuress worked out to maintain her physique.

Matilda the White Lady and her husband joined several other aging adventurers on a quest that ended up dragging them across several worlds, including Olympus, where they met the deity Hermes; the jungles of Quorsit; and the demi-plane of Kansas, where she faced a powerful fighter Maralix in a duel and survived.

## Manycoins House

Manycoins House, sometime misnamed as Moneycoins House, was a templed dedicated to Waukeen, the Merchant's Friend, and the Merchants' League offices, located in the Lower City of Baldur's Gate.

Location
Manycoins House stood on an intersection of Stormshore Street and Hammaskarl's Ride, just two blocks away from the Basilisk Gate in the Eastway neighborhood of the Lower City.

Structure
The large temple structure was roughly L-shaped and was a four-story building with an attic space where the temple's dormers were located. The building also included stall stables and roofed coach storage available to the customers and guests.

Services
The temple provided all the regular religious Waukeenar services. Additionally, the complex offered secure rental-stall stables and coach storage, as well as short-term rental lodgings primarily used to conduct business in Baldur's Gate. Each of these lodgings included a bedroom chamber, a bathing chamber, and a "trading chamber" – spaced used for business meetings and negotiations. Guests received laundering and bathing services, as well as bread and water. Despite the lack of meals, guests were given access to oven facilities. Renting was priced at a single silver coin and an offering to Waukeen.

Among religious services, Manycoins House offered training to lay people and novice priests of Waukeen. Little advertised offerings included privacy of many undisclosed secret passages and discrete paid vaults for storing of small items of any nature.

## Malakar Surth

Malakar Surth was a merchant from Marsember in the late 14 century DR.

Description
Malakar Surth sounded sour and sarcastic, often speaking with a thin voice. He was a lean, tall man. His face was hard and thin.

Personality
Malakar was a sarcastic, insensitive man with a superior attitude and a cruel, sadistic streak.

Possessions
Malakar and Bezrar both had Marsemban long knifes, often used for gutting fish, but also for combat.

Of note, Malakar Surth owned a coach, stables, and two dapple gray draft horses. His house was very private, and contained numerous traps.

Activities
Malakar dealt in alcohol, drugs, perfumes, and poisons, often with spell-wielding outlanders.

Relationships
Aumun Tholant Bezrar and Malakar Surth were known to have worked together, and it was believed by Durexter Dagohnlar that Malakar was the leader, while Bezrar was not as bold without him. Malakar knew that Aumun was infatuated with a dancer at the Amorous Anchor.

Malakar Surth had recently come to be associated with a Red Wizard of Thay, Harnrim Starangh. He also appeared to be aware of someone known as Ponczer at the Firehelm.

History
As of the early spring of, Malakar Surth and Aumun Tholant Bezrar had both been swindled of 10,000 gp by Durexter Dagohnlar.

At the Dagohnlars' bedroom, they were able to get in undetected, then attack while the married couple was unclad, and otherwise engaged in bed, attacking with surprise. Aumun Tholant Bezrar, after choking Durexter, captured Starmara; while binding her, Malakar Surth noticed she had a tattoo. Their two victims were first tied up on the rug, and then tied to the bedposts. They were distracted by Narnra Shalace, a thief, bursting into the room through the window, seeking to escape a pursuing Harper, Glarasteer Rhauligan.

Glarasteer made quick work of the two: Aumun Tholant Bezrar fled after sustaining minor injuries, while Malakar Surth was pinned under a chest that fell atop his head, knocked out, and promptly ignored by the Harper. After he healed Narnra, she fled too, making him leave the scene to resume his pursuit. Durexter and Starmara Dagohnlar tried to free themselves and kill Malakar Surth.

Malakar got up to see the first rays of dawn, and managed to free himself before Starmara and Durexter released themselves. As he had an appointment early in the morning, he fled the house at full speed rather than eliminate them, suffering numerous accidents as he descended the stairs. He found Aumun Tholant Bezrar waiting for him at the door, with a coach car, warm towels, and a change of clothes, all of which were actually Malakar Surth's; he wondered briefly how come the man had known of those or managed to get his hands on them, given his house was trapped and never visited.

The coach drove them to Haelithtorntowers, where Harnrim Starangh had wanted them for meeting Lady Joysil Ambrur. They remained with Harnrim Starangh through the meeting, though they hardly spoke; they both heard that Vangerdahast had retired to a sanctum near Mouth o' Gargoyles, where he hoped to complete a certain task and maybe sire a heir.

They were summoned at a later date by Harnrim Starangh, who provided them with a bag of explosive devices and compelled them to pursue Vangerdahast with a spell, destroying any helmed horrors on the way to the sanctum by using the aforementioned devices. He then teleported them near the sanctum. The two of them started on their path, though they were disoriented and suspicious of their own actions, yet powerless not to follow the path before them. They continued to follow the path, attacking the helmed horrors before them with explosives, until they were attacked by a War Wizard sentry, Pheldemar, and fled.

The two made it back to Marsember, where they took refuge in the upper floors of a warehouse, near a box of Selgauntan glowstones, which Malakar believed would make them impossible to find by magic. While in there, they eavesdropped on two nobles, Thaedro and Sauvrurn, and learned that the ruffians owning that warehouse, almost certainly they themselves, were sought by the authorities and had been for many days. Learning of the Rightful Conspiracy and their plan to kill Filfaeril Obarskyr and Alusair Obarskyr, they decided instead to leave Marsember entirely.

Shortly after they boarded a ship bound for Sembia, continuing to banter throughout the trip. While on the ship, they witnessed a fang dragon with a swath of rainbow-colored scales on its flank, which interrupted one of their fights. Surth considered leaving for Yhaunn, Westgate, or the Pirate Isles, to get away from Red Wizards; Bezrar was just glad they wouldn't see Harnrim Starangh again. Unknown to them, Harnrim was aboard the same ship, transformed into a ballast-stone, also trying to escape scrutiny.

## Mangee

Mangee used a ten-sided board to play the game and needed a full set of twenty-five pieces. Each game piece was an expertly carved jade figurine of a creature, and each was enchanted with alteration, enchantment, and conjuration magics and was valued at 500 gold pieces. The figurines' magic could only be used if all the pieces were assembled together, and no divination sorcery could reveal the magic before the set was completed.

Some of the jade figurines were: a dragon, a lion, an eagle, a monkey, and a bear.

History
The origins of Mangee were obscure but traceable to the Empire of Shou Lung in Kara-Tur, long before the 14 century DR. An incomplete set of figurines was recovered in the mid-to-late 14 century DR by a band of heroes of the Living City. The Mangee statuettes were hidden in a cave in the mountains on the Vast inhabited by deadly creatures like chimerae and manticores.

Services
This shop specialized in selling material components for spells. The owner would claim that the prices offered for these components were far fairer than those in Ravens Bluff's marketplace, referring to the merchants there as being practically "thieves".

History
Around the late 14 century DR, a group of adventurers came to the Flask Circle in search of supplies for the alchemist Wendell. When they entered Tarwell was rather pleased to see them. They showed him their shopping list, causing the former wizard to put on a robe and scrounge through its many pockets. Within them Tarwell was able to find a crushed emerald, some jamain root, maple leaves, and sulfurous ash, but lacked any hair from bookas. He attempted to cast some form of conjuration spell to bring forth a booka, but it strained him too much.

Overall Tarwell charged the party sixteen gold pieces for the components. He then offered them directions to Anderson Farm, claiming that the adventurers could find some bookas there.

In, during the aftermath of the massacre during the Council of the Dragon in late Mirtul of the, the War Wizard Surgol Velard had the intruder and mask dancer Amarune Whitewave, whom he had incapacitated with a wand of sleep, moved to the Mages' Dutychamber, where he planned to search her for weapons personally.

While he wondered how to undo her clothes, the Marchioness Immerdusk, Storm Silverhand, listened to the door, and decided, together with her companion Mirt, to stop him; Mirt went to the far door and banged on it, distracting him. While he turned, the Silverhand sister ran into the room and knocked him out cold. She then rescued Amarune Whitewave.

## Maug graft

Maug grafts were special grafts created for the purpose of augmenting maug warriors. While intended for constructs, it was possible to attach them onto other creatures as well.

Description
Generally, they were crafted from metal or the stone of Thuldanin, the second layer of the plane of Acheron. Once attached, maug grafts did not radiate magic, and they could generally not be reused if removed.

Creation
Only maugs understood how such grafts were created, and in particular they were applied by maug spellcasters, such as the ancient Thulkarr. Transforming a creature using maug grafts required experience as a healer, specialized knowledge of how to attach grafts, and often access to one or more relevant spells. The grafts could be sized for even very tiny and very massive recipients.

Users
New maugs received a simple graft upon their creation—such as a locking hand, shoving arm, or stone spitter—and experienced maug mercenaries would use their amassed treasure to pay for additional upgrades. Maug spellcasters also devised ways to augment creatures of flesh with these grafts, although they reserved such transformations for their followers.

History
In, two maug fighters sporting shoving arm grafts served the Zhentarim as guardians at Castle Krag in Shadowdale.

Notable Maug Grafts
Locking hand
A stone hand that replaced an existing hand. The fingers were designed to lock together, granting the recipient creature an extraordinarily strong grip, however the use of the hand was dexterous enough not to inhibit fine motor control (such as spellcasting gestures).
Rollers
A creature's legs were replaced by a stone pyramid with six heavy cylinders. This graft limited the creature's mobility to rolling, but could be used to crush enemies.
Shoving arm
A large piston ending in an open, upright hand replaced an existing arm and was secured to a creature's torso with a stone strap. This arm and hand were useless for most activities save for forcefully pushing or striking enemies or objects.
Shudder plate
A stone frame was embedded in a creature (usually in the chest) and held a thin square of enchanted shale that would quietly vibrate in tune with the environment, granting a form of tremorsense.
Spike stones
Small round stones were embedded all over a creature's surface. On command, the creature could cause these to elongate into sharp, armor-piercing spikes.
Stone spitter
A box was affixed to a creature's shoulder with a thin tube extending from the base. This contraption could be used to fire bullets at supernaturally high speeds. It could hold up to 50 bullets at a time, but could only be used to unload its ammunition six times per day.

## Maug (construct)

Maugs were constructs from the plane of Acheron that served as perfect mercenaries in battles across the planes. They were intelligent and tireless soldiers willing to serve any employer.

Description
Maugs were hulking,  humanoid constructs made of  of steel-gray Acheron stone. Because of their bulk, they could not run. Their bodies were often augmented with stone or metal grafts, and were armored with heavy iron breastplates. They preferred to wield massive two-bladed swords.

As constructs, they did not sleep, were immune to mind-affecting magic, were unaffected by poisons or diseases, could not be magically paralyzed or weakened, and necromancy did not affect them. They were ageless and could only die if destroyed in battle. A maug had no soul and could not be raised from death. If they sustained battle damage, they could slowly repair themselves by resting, although this process could not restore lost limbs.

Personality

Fighting gave meaning to a maug's existence. They were fearless and approached any conflict as if it were a battle in a war, thus requiring a strategy.

They did not care about the morality of the causes for which they fought, and were unwaveringly loyal to their employers, however they would would not fight other maugs. If two opposing armies both hired maugs, casualties would be extraordinary as they ignored each other to cut swathes through their respective enemies. Once one side was finally unable to continue the fight, the maugs would all band together to seek their next job.

Combat
Maugs were unflinchingly in battle and would charge straight into conflict. That said, they always devised a plan for any engagement, and would try to control the flow of any battle. If they had advance knowledge of a fight, they would prepare the battlefield with traps and earthworks or would find opportunities to conceal themselves by camouflaging among rocks or rubble.

Three times each day, maugs had the ability to negate the hardness of any object up to  in size. Skilled maug warriors would use this power to render brittle the armor and weapons of their foes before sundering them into pieces.

Maug arcane spellcasters made use of magic that could repair maugs' construct bodies in much the same way as divine healing magic might cure injuries of flesh and blood.

Society
They hailed from Acheron, specifically their fortress in the second layer, Thuldanin, to which they were had been exiled in the distant past. From there, they ventured out to accept mercenary contracts. Maugs acted alone, in small squads, or in larger warbands or organized companies of 40 or more individuals. Their larger units had officers and hierarchy, and often incorporated hobgoblin troops as well. The service of a maug mercenary was at least 5 gp per day (more if the mercenary had more experience) and payment was generally expected up-front in the form of magic items or rare ores.

Outside of Acheron, maugs might be encountered on the Material Plane, where they were known to wander for centuries as they sought wars in which to serve.

Maugs often trained as fighters, but could excel in any discipline. Spellcasters were often sorcerers or wizards who specialized in travelling the planes or crafting new maugs. Clerics and druids were rare among maugs owing to their lack of souls or connections to the natural world, and so the sorcerers and wizards fulfilled the roles of healers. Thanks to their mechanical construction, maugs had an innate understanding of topics in engineering, stonemasonry, and architecture.

Thulkarr
The Thulkarr were the leaders of the maugs. They were ancient spellcasters credited with being the original maugs as well as the ones who had created most living maugs. While they were widely respected as generals and creators, the Thulkarr gave few orders and instead focused on making sure their fellow maugs continued to serve others in battle. They would negotiate for the best possible terms for maug mercenaries and travelled the planes looking for conflicts worthy of maug service. Upon finding one, they would open gates for their troops.

The Thulkarr were also known to charge coin from their maugs in exchange for various services in order to afford the costs of creating new maugs.

Creation

The secrets of maug creation were known only to the Thulkarr. They were crafted on Acheron out of that plane's pitiless rock in a process that cost at least 10,000 gp. Upon creation, many maugs were granted a minor grafted limb or weapon carved from the stone of Thuldanin in a procedure that cost an additional 2,000 gp. As a maug gained wealth from their mercenary services, some would purchase additional grafts.

History
Scholars believed that maugs had originally served as shock troops in the Great Conflagration, fighting on behalf of Raumathar under the leadership of a war-leader named Thulkarr. Their armies used portals to outflank their Nar enemies and drive them back until the Nentyarch unleashed a final gambit known as the Dark Fissure, which opened a planar rift that banished the whole army. While initially prisoners in Thuldanin, they soon turned it into their fortress. The original maug spellcasters adopted the name of Thulkarr and used knowledge stolen from their creators to begin making more of their kind, and in turn came to be regarded as the leaders of the maugs.

As of the late 14 century DR, rumors persisted that old ruins in northeast Faerûn might contain either the secrets to creating maugs and/or the rites to banish them to Acheron once more.

In, maug fighters served the Zhentarim as guardians at Castle Krag in Shadowdale.

## Malthrox's Shadowcaster

Malthrox's Shadowcaster was a magical lantern.

Description
Malthrox's Shadowcaster appeared to be an ordinary oil lantern made of bluish metal, featuring shutters on all four sides. The lantern had a wooden handle with a bone grip. Two of the shutters bore inscriptions, which could only be read using read magic. When handled by anyone other than a mage, Malthrox's Shadowcaster functioned as a regular lantern. However, when held by a mage, its powers were communicated telepathically.

Abilities
The runes inscribed on the outside of the shutters read "Bizzait" and "Missathac." When only the shutter marked "Bizzait" was opened and the word was spoken, the narrow beam of light produced had the power to dispel magic. This power could be used three times per day. The area of effect encompassed a  area upon which the lantern's light first fell, including any creatures within this area, with a range of . Interestingly, beyond this range, the light beam maintained the same diameter, although it was roughly conical before that point.

When the word "Missathac" was uttered and the corresponding shutter was opened, a  bright beam of light flashed forward, striking the nearest object within a  range. If the beam hit a living creature, it produced a shadowclone.

The shadowclone was a spectral replica of the creature caught in the lantern's beam. This clone mirrored the original in terms of size, speed, and held weapons, but with notable differences. The shadowclone was incapable of casting spells or using psionics, and any magical items it duplicated were devoid of magical properties. The clone could only be harmed by weapons that were enchanted, though it remained susceptible to spells unless they were countered by the clone's magic resistance.

The shadowclone was completely under the control of the lantern bearer, requiring the bearer's concentration to remain active. If the bearer's concentration was interrupted, either by a successful attack or other disturbances, the clone was dispelled. This power was limited to once per week. If any other shutters were open when the command was spoken, the power did not activate.

## Malphagor

Malphagor was a Tanar'ri Prince and an upstart deity of the undead worshiped in the Underdark region underneath the Vast, who sought to usurp undead the portfolio from Orcus and the necromancy portfolio from Velsharoon.

Description
Followers of the deity believed that raising the undead was giving them the "Blessing of Malphagor" and the dead individual souls were gifts to the god who, in exchange, gives them eternal unlife. The center of Malphagorian worship was located on the far side of the Sea of Endless Darkness in relation to Ravens Bluff, about a month's time travel.

History
Malphagor's cult became a common knowledge after the expedition from Ravens Bluff descended into the Underdark and established the Ravens Deep settlement in the . Expedition members ran into several powerful cultists of Malphagor near the Watch Post Cavern, led by Filas, a ranking human lich priest of the upstart deity. The war band under Filas's, leadership consisted of Angor, a dwarven death knight and its eight dwarven skeleton warriors, Dannon, a dwarf vampire, and two of his thralls. The group set out to fight and kill a best of beholders and raise them as more of the undead followers of Malphagor. Despite their undead existence, the Malphagorians sought no trouble with the living Ravenaar and only wanted a passage to their secret mark. Only if the living were to promise their "destiny" to Malphagor would Filas reveal the group's true goals.

By the late 14 century DR, relatively recently before 1370 DR, the island town of Tradesport in the Sea of Endless Darkness faced an undead incursion. Several of the city's Trading Houses used undead workers, who rebelled when an ancient hidden crypt, part of the ancient temple of Set, opened, unleashing its shambling guardians. The unquiet dead began slaughtering everyone in their way, and only with the arrival of Malphagor's priests the undead were pacified and forced under the priests' control. The clergy of Malphagor demanded a section of the city to be given to them as payment. Since then, Malphagor's followers had been an integral part of the city's commerce, trading in the undead servants created from the slaves exported out of Thay. Inhabitants of Tradesport showed no love for the deity's clergy nor for the god's undead servants. The Wail of the Banshee, a necromancer's ship made of bone, operated out of Tradesport with its master, a drow necromancer named Mezzalcat serving Malphagor.

Circa 1370 DR, the Cult of the Dragon, namely Shalimarra Daradusk of Ravens Bluff, allied with the clergy of Malphagor in the Vast, using the god's priest to help them raise white dragons as undead. During the same period of time, powerful priests of Malphagor visited the site of a great battle between drow and duergar in the Lower Sarbreen to collect bodies of the dead to be risen as servants of their deity. The human lich priest, Velcrest, showed no desire to fight adventurers from Ravens Bluff who came across the grim scavenging and, if left unprovoked, was happy to share information about his patron deity.

## Mardasper Oblyndrin

Mardasper Oblyndrin was a wizard and a Guardian of Moonshorn Tower of the mid–8 century DR.

Description
He was middling in age, handsome, with sharp sideburns and raven-black hair. His eyes were deep brown, but one of them was white and glowing, like a blazing star, which never closed.

Personality
He liked to daydream at length, and sometimes drank hard drinks, despite the fact that any day in which hard drink passed through his lips was not a day counted toward his service to the tower.

Abilities
One spell he wielded was shatterstar. His accursed eye could see things that even detecting spells missed, and his Guardianship afforded him control over the wards of Moonshorn. His magic proved insufficient to break the spell upon his eye. He was loath to engage in spell duels, even against lesser foes.

Possessions
As the Guardian of Moonshorn Tower, he was granted use of the Lady Scepter and a matching diadem, which had an eyepiece suitable for covering his odd eye.

Activities
As of early spring in, Mardasper had been the guardian of Moonshorn Tower for two years. All entered were to work no magic unbidden and to surrender all written or embodied magic to him. Their possessions would be returned upon leaving.

Relationships
He dealt at a distance with Tabarast and Beldrune, two scholars at the Tower.

History
Mardasper was cursed with his blazing eye after or during a spell duel. Furthermore, Mardasper had been witness to the previous guardian of Moonshorn being disintegrated after mishandling the Lady Scepter.

In the, Mardasper Oblyndrin began his guardianship of Moonshorn Tower; he was promised that upon completion of four years of service, the spell upon his eye would be broken by the priests of Mystra. Two years later, in the, he greeted Elminster Aumar, an undercover Chosen of Mystra, upon his passage through Moonshorn Tower.

Later that evening, Ilbryn Starym crossed the doors of Moonshorn Tower, and refused to comply with any of the Guardian's instructions; when he asked about Elminster's name in the visitor's log, Mardasper told him that the man had already left. Trying to regain some dignity, Mardasper offered to leave a message for Elminster, should he ever return. Ilbryn accepted; however, Mardasper suspected that had gone badly. Retreating to his office, he asked Mystra for a sign while uncorking a dusty bottle he'd hidden behind three voluminous tomes. The sign he received, if any, was the cork slamming itself back into the bottle so violently that it drew blood from his fingers. Mardasper remained unsure if that was a good or bad sign.

Mardasper was watching from the top of the tower when the wards warned him of uncontrolled power, shortly after, as the Slayer burst into the tower. Though Mardasper wasn't able to spot the entity even with the wards, he suspected that it was inside, and sealed the doors before walking up into the collection. Peering through the keyhole, he spotted the misty entity drinking the power from the assorted enchanted trinkets there. He burst through the door casting a shatterstar spell, but despite it being sufficient for targeting the ghostly creature, it endured the attack and responded with an acidic spell that slew him.

## Maethor

Maethor was a Baron of Galadorna during the mid–8 century DR.

He was known to be silver-tongued, and was called a pretty boy at least once. He dressed richly, with a ruffled cloak, and had a perfect flowing mane of brown hair.

Relationships

History
In the, Baron Maethor supported the bid of Baron Tholone to ascend to the throne of Galadorna, in exchange for Baron Belundrar to take up service as seneschal. Feldrin, in turn, agreed to support Tholone's bid as well, in exchange for Maethor's future assassination. In any event, this did not materialize as the King and Tholone were both eliminated by Court Mage Ilgrist right in the middle of pronouncing Tholone king. As Ilgrist revealed himself to be Nadrathen, only to be eliminated by two newly arriving mages, Elminster Aumar and Dasumia, Maethor briefly considered backstabbing Elminster. He decided against it as Dasumia crowned herself Queen of Galadorna, and then ordered her apprentice Elminster to bring her a vow of loyalty or a vital organ from every surviving baron.

Up until the later destruction of Galadorna, Maethor was still alive, and still known for his love of poison and intrigue.

Rumors
He was seen as a man who spun a thousand intrigues, and danced in as many bedchambers.
